Tria ergo a discipulis hic requi- rit arctissimae vitae magister optimus et doctor; nam, sicut tria sunt praecipue docentis munia, ut scilicet doceat, delectet et flectat, ut scribit Augustinus (Lib. ivde Doctrina Christ. cap. 12); ita tria sunt etiam discipulorum auditorumque officia, ut nempe auscultent docentem, libenter excipiant delectantem, et efficaciter compleant id ad quod flectit orator, quae tria respexisse visus est S.
passages.english: you will meet, carry out the Lord's precepts that you have heard. Here, then, the excellent master and teacher of the strictest life requires three things of his disciples. For just as there are three chief duties of one who teaches, namely that he should teach, delight and move, as Augustine writes (On Christian Doctrine, book 4, chapter 12), so there are also three duties of disciples and hearers: that they listen attentively to the one teaching, receive gladly the one delighting, and effectively fulfil that to which the speaker moves [them]. These three St.

passages.original: viri Verbis colligere possumus, magis ad discendam obe- dientiam 9 quam ad peragendam poenitentiam Re- gulae hujus schola cognoscitur instituta, non ut, sive peccatores, sive justos excludat, vel unum genus hominum respuat, sed quia omnem vini et intentio- nem ad edocenda obedientiae praecepta constituat. » Et sane cum coenobitarum monachorum fortissimum genus sibi disponendum proposuerit S. Pater, non alium prorsus ab ipso coenobitarum fine intendere debuit; quis autem ille sit docet apud Cassianum ab- bas Joannes his verbis (Collat, 19, c. 8); « Finis coenobitae est omnes suas mortificare et crucifigere voluntates; » et Severus Sulpicius (Dial. lib. i, c 5) :·’ « Haec illorum prima virtus parere alieno imperio; ». tandem S. Hieronymus de Coenobitis scribens : (Epist. 22) : « Prima, inquit, apud eos confoederatio, est obedire majoribus, et quidquid jusserint facere.» Eadem habet Regula S. Posthumio ab angelo tradita n. i, prout exstat in ejus Vita, cap, 8. Hinc vix ul- lum in tota S. P. Bened cti Regula caput exstat in quo obedientiam aliquo modo non commendet, ut facili negotio demonstrare possemus, nisi id muneris ante nos obiisset vir doctissimus Benedictus Haefte- nus in Disquisitionibus monasticis I.
passages.english: man's words we can gather, the school of this Rule is known to have been instituted more for learning obedience than for performing penance; not so as to exclude either sinners or the just, or to reject any one kind of men, but because it sets its whole force and intention on teaching the precepts of obedience." And indeed, since the holy Father had proposed to himself to regulate the strongest kind of monks, the cenobites, he ought to have intended no other end at all than the very end of cenobites. What that end is, Abbot John teaches in Cassian in these words (Conferences 19, chapter 8): "The end of the cenobite is to mortify and crucify all his own wills"; and Sulpicius Severus (Dialogues, book 1, chapter 5): "This is their first virtue, to obey another's command"; and finally St. Jerome, writing of the cenobites (Letter 22): "Their first compact," he says, "is to obey their elders and to do whatever they have ordered." The Rule handed down to St. Posthumius by an angel has the same, no. 1, as it stands in his Life, chapter 8. Hence there is scarcely any chapter in the whole Rule of the holy Father Benedict in which he does not in some way commend obedience, as we could easily demonstrate, had not that most learned man Benedict van Haeften already discharged this task before us in his Monastic Disquisitions I
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence, continuing a quotation of Peter Damian ('Quantum ergo ex S. viri verbis...': 'So far as we can gather from the holy man's words'). 'vini' read as 'vim'. The stray '9' is a footnote mark. 'Posthumius' (Pachomius?) not securely identified.

passages.original: Excitante nos Scriptura ac dicente : « Hora est jam nunc de somno surgere. » Jam nunc, id est eo ipso quo loquor tempore, sine ulla prorsus dilatione : quia, ut dicit apud Cassianum abbas Germanus (Col- lat. 17, cap. 5), « ad profectum spiritualium rerum, virtutemque tendentibus periculosa ac noxia est et parva dilatio; » et, ut ait S. Ambros us (In c. iLuc.), « nescit tarda molimina Spiritus sancti gratia. »
passages.english: Scripture rousing us and saying: "It is now the hour to rise from sleep." "Now", that is, at the very time in which I speak, without any delay at all: because, as Abbot Germanus says in Cassian (Conferences 17, chapter 5), "for those striving toward progress in spiritual things and toward virtue, even a small delay is dangerous and harmful"; and, as St. Ambrose says (On Luke, chapter 1), "the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow efforts."

passages.original: sed haec figurate dicta sunt, et secundum nostrum loquendi modum; « quibusque autem nominatis Dei membris, quae in nobis visibilia et corporea sunt, potentias operatio- num oportet intelligi, » inquit Augustinus (In psal. ix); et sic oculi Domini aliquando pro ejus cogni- tione, ut cum S. Benedictus dicit oculos Domini in omni loco speculari bonos et malos; aliquando pro justo ejus in malos judicio, ut cum dicitur in psalmo : Vultus autem Domini super facientes mala, ut perdat de terra memoriam eorum; aliquando pro pia in bonos misericordia, ut cum propheta dicit : Oculi Domini super justos, etc., quo sensu oculi Domini hic accipiendi sunt, quibus utinam miseros nos pec- catores respiciat!
passages.english: but these things are said figuratively and according to our manner of speaking. "Whenever members of God are named which in us are visible and bodily, we must understand the powers of his operations," says Augustine (On Psalm 9). And so "the eyes of the Lord" stand sometimes for his knowledge, as when St. Benedict says that the eyes of the Lord in every place behold the good and the wicked; sometimes for his just judgement on the wicked, as when it is said in the psalm: But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth; sometimes for his loving mercy toward the good, as when the prophet says: The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, etc. In this sense the eyes of the Lord are to be taken here; with them may he look upon us wretched sinners!

passages.original: Qui non egit dolum in lingua sua.] Ad quae verba iterum S. Augustinus : « Lingua agitur dolus, cum aliud ore profertur et aliud pectore tegitur. »
passages.english: Who has not practised deceit with his tongue.] On these words St. Augustine again [says]: "Deceit is practised with the tongue when one thing is uttered by the mouth and another is hidden in the heart."

passages.original: Qui opprobrium non accepit adversus proximum suum.] Id est « non libenter aut temere credidit criminatori, » ut ait S. Augustinus (In psalxiv ). Aliam hujus versiculi expositionem ex S. Hieronymo tradit Hildemarus; « Ille, inquit, non accipit oppro- brium adversus proximum suum, qui nullum laesit, neminem nocuit, neminem scandalizavit, ut ab illo debuisset accipere opprobrium. »
passages.english: Who has not taken up a reproach against his neighbour.] That is, "has not willingly or rashly believed an accuser," as St. Augustine says (On Psalm 14). Hildemar gives another explanation of this verse from St. Jerome: "He does not take up a reproach against his neighbour," he says, "who has injured no one, harmed no one, scandalised no one, such that he should have received reproach from him."

passages.original: Et iterum ipse dicit : Qui gloriatur in Domino glo- rietur.] Gloriari in Domino est omnem hom operis gloriam ei attribuere, ut cum Paphnutio abbate apud Cassianum (Collat.iii, c. 15), bona nostra demiran- tibus, atque inde laude nos efferentibus dicere pos- simus : « Non liberum arbitrium, sed Dominus solvit compeditos; non nostra virtus, sed Dominus erigit elisos; non lectionis industria, sed Dominus illuminat caecos, quod Graece dicitur κύριος σοφοί τύφλους, id est Dominus sapientes facit caecos; non nostra cautio, sed Dominus custodit advenas; non nostra fortitudo, sed Dominus allevat sive suffulcit omnes qui cor- ruunt, etc.;
passages.english: And again he himself says: Let him who glories glory in the Lord.] To glory in the Lord is to attribute to him all the glory of good work, so that, with Abbot Paphnutius in Cassian (Conferences 3, chapter 15), we may say to those who marvel at our good deeds and therefore extol us with praise: "Not free will, but the Lord frees the fettered; not our virtue, but the Lord raises up the crushed; not diligence in reading, but the Lord gives light to the blind, which in Greek is said κύριος σοφοί τύφλους, that is, the Lord makes the blind wise; not our caution, but the Lord guards the strangers; not our strength, but the Lord lifts up or supports all who fall, etc.;
passages.notes: 'hom' read as 'boni'. The Greek is garbled (presumably κύριος σοφοῖ τυφλούς, 'the Lord makes the blind wise'); translated per the Latin gloss.

passages.original: Et quod minus habet in nobis natura possibile.] Illud quod potest hic sumi adverbialiter, ut sensus sit : et quia ad regni coelestis consecutionem, et ad praeparanda corda et corpora nostra sanctae praece- ptorum obedientiae militatura, in nobis natura hu- mana per peccatum depravata et corrupta minus habet possibile, id est ex se nihil potest : nam, ut observat ad hunc locum Menardus noster, minus apud Tullium saepe significat non.
passages.english: And what nature has less possible in us.] That 'quod' can here be taken adverbially, so that the sense is: and because, for attaining the heavenly kingdom and for preparing our hearts and bodies to do service in holy obedience to the precepts, human nature in us, depraved and corrupted by sin, has less possible, that is, can do nothing of itself: for, as our Ménard observes on this passage, 'minus' in Cicero often means 'not'.
passages.notes: 'quod' taken adverbially = 'because'; the Latin 'minus... possibile' cannot be fully reproduced in English.

passages.original: neque omnino insolitum est apud veteres scripta sacra institutaque sanctorum scholas appellare; nam et S. Hieronymus, referente Boherio, in epist. ad Evagrium librum Exodi vocat scholam medici, ubi leges datae a Deo populo Israel sunt descriptae; et interrogatus apud Cassianum Joannes abbas, cur, relicta anachoresi, coenobitarem instituta esset am- plexus, respondit, « velut imparem se anachore- ticae disciplinae, et sublimitate tantae perfectionis in- dignum ad juniorum scholas revertisse, si tamen vel ipsorum instituta secundum professionis meritum posset implere.
passages.english: nor is it at all unusual among the ancients to call sacred writings and the institutes of the saints 'schools'; for St. Jerome too, as Boherius reports, in his letter to Evagrius calls the book of Exodus a 'physician's school', where the laws given by God to the people of Israel are written down; and Abbot John, asked in Cassian why, having left the anchoritic life, he had embraced the cenobitic institutes, replied that "as one unequal to the anchoritic discipline and unworthy of the loftiness of so great a perfection, he had returned to the schools of the juniors, if indeed he could fulfil even their institutes according to the merit of his profession.
passages.notes: 'Boherius' not securely identified.

passages.original: 8, saec.iiBened.) cum obstanti matri, et limini ostii inhaerenti, postularet ut se ad monasterium ire sine- ret, illaque ejulans et pavimento prostrata denega- ret se permissuram : « Ille enim limen matremque transiliens, poposcit matrem ne moerore solveretur, dicens se nunquam deinceps in hac vita videndum. » Ad hujusmodi crudelitatem nos etiam hortatur pro- pheta cum dicit: Obliviscere populum tuum et domum patris tui, et concupiscet Rex decorem tuum; ad quod attendens S. Hieronymus exclamat (Epist. 10, ad Furiam) : « Grande praemium parentis obliti : Et concupiscet Rex decorem tuum. »
passages.english: 8, 2nd century of the Benedictines), when, his mother resisting and clinging to the threshold of the door, he asked her to let him go to the monastery, and she, wailing and lying prostrate on the floor, refused to allow it: "He, leaping over the threshold and his mother, asked his mother not to be undone by grief, saying that she would never see him again in this life." The prophet also urges us to cruelty of this kind when he says: Forget your people and your father's house, and the King will desire your beauty; attending to which St. Jerome exclaims (Letter 10, to Furia): "Great is the reward of having forgotten a parent: And the King will desire your beauty."
passages.notes: Begins mid-reference (Jonas, Life of St. Columbanus, no. 8, in Acta Sanctorum O.S.B., saec. II).

passages.original: Monachorum.] Monachus dicitur ille qui segrega- tus ab omni hominum frequentia, in solitudine poe- nitentiae lacrymis vacat, et Deo totus adhaerens, unus cum eo spiritus efficitur, ut vel ipsa nominis ejus etymologia indicat : nam monachus a verbo graeco μόνος, id est unus, dicitur : hinc canon ille concilii Nicaeni a Gratiano citatus : « Placuit omnibus residen- tibus in sancta Nicaena synodo ut monachorum con- versatio et vita secundum etymologiam nominis ab omnibus discrepet (Monachus enim Graece, Latine singularis dicitur) : unde monachum per omnia sin- gulariter agere oportet. » Et S. Hieronymus ad He- liodorum scribens (Epist.i) : « Interpretare vocabu- lum monachi, hoc est tuum; quid facis in turba, qui solus es? » et ad Rusticum monachum (Epist. 4) : « Quid desideramus urbium frequentiam, qui de sin- gularitate censemur? » et ad Paulinum (Epist. 13) : « Si cupis esse quod diceris, id est solus, quid facis in urbibus, quae utique non sunt solorum habitacula, sed multorum?
passages.english: Of monks.] A monk is said to be one who, separated from all the company of men, gives himself in solitude to the tears of penance, and, cleaving wholly to God, becomes one spirit with him, as even the etymology of his name shows: for "monk" is said from the Greek word μόνος, that is "one." Hence that canon of the Council of Nicaea cited by Gratian: "It pleased all those sitting in the holy synod of Nicaea that the conduct and life of monks should differ from all others according to the etymology of the name (for 'monachus' in Greek is called 'singularis' in Latin); hence a monk ought to act singly in all things." And St Jerome, writing to Heliodorus (Epist. 1): "Interpret the word 'monk', that is, your own [name]; what are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?" And to Rusticus the monk (Epist. 4): "Why do we long for the crowds of cities, we who are reckoned by our singleness?" And to Paulinus (Epist. 13): "If you desire to be what you are called, that is, alone, what are you doing in cities, which are certainly the dwellings not of those who are alone, but of many?

passages.original: 1): « Triplex omnino est omnis religiosae vitae ratio : ut vel solus et solitarius decer- tando vivas, vel 40 cum uno alterove sodali, vel ut in coenobio cum pluribus per patientiam conquiescas. Primo enim denotat anachoretas, qui soli; secundo sarabaitas, qui bini aut terni; tertio coenobitas, qui cum pluribus degunt. Sed et apud Cassianum abbas Piamon eadem tria monachorum genera in Aegypto exstitisse testatur (Collat. 18, cap. 4) : « quorum duo sunt optima, inquit, tertium vero tepidum et omni modis evitandum. » Quartum addit ejusdem collatio nis cap.
passages.english: 1): "There is in all a threefold pattern of every religious life: either that you live alone and solitary in struggle, or with one or two companions, or that you find rest through patience in a cenobium with many." For by the first he denotes the anchorites, who [live] alone; by the second the sarabaites, who [live] in twos or threes; by the third the cenobites, who live with many. But in Cassian too Abbot Piamun testifies that the same three kinds of monks existed in Egypt (Conference 18, ch. 4): "of which two," he says, "are the best, but the third is lukewarm and to be avoided in every way." He adds a fourth in chapter
passages.notes: The opening "1)" completes a citation of John Climacus (Step 1) begun in the preceding context. The stray "40" is a page number and has been omitted. The chapter number follows in the next passage ("8").

passages.original: Primum institutione, ut pote quod a primis Eccle- siae temporibus sumpsi se dicitur exordium; nam, ut tradit apud Cassianum abbas Piamon (Collat. 48, c. 5), « talis tunc erat omnis Ecclesia, quales nunc perpaucos in coenobiis invenire difficile est; sed cum post apostolorum excessum tepescere coepisset mul- titudo credentium,.... hi quibus adhuc erat aposto- licus fervor, memores pristinae illius perfectionis, discedentes a civitatibus suis, illorumque consortio qui sibi vel Ecclesiae Dei remissioris vitae negligen- tiam illicitam esse credebant, in locis suburbanis ac secretioribus commanere, et ea quae ab apostolis per universum corpus Ecclesiae generaliter meminerant instituta privatim exercere coeperunt;
passages.english: First in institution, inasmuch as it is said to have taken its beginning from the first times of the Church; for, as Abbot Piamun relates in Cassian (Conference 18, ch. 5), "the whole Church was then such as it is now difficult to find [even] a very few in cenobia; but when, after the death of the apostles, the multitude of believers had begun to grow lukewarm, .... those in whom the apostolic fervour still remained, mindful of that former perfection, departing from their cities and from the company of those who believed that the negligence of a laxer life was permitted to themselves or to the Church of God, began to dwell in places near the cities and more secluded, and to practise privately those things which they remembered had been instituted by the apostles generally throughout the whole body of the Church;
passages.notes: The edition prints "Collat. 48"; this is evidently a misreading of 18, and 18 has been translated. "Sumpsi se" has been read as "sumpsisse." The clause "quales nunc perpaucos ... invenire difficile est" is compressed in the Latin, and the rendering is approximate.

passages.original: » Et sane mona- sterii vocem ad solam unius monachi habitationem designandam frequenter usurpari in 42 sanctorum Patrum Vitis constat : unde S. Athanasius in Vita S. Antonii (Cap. 21) : « Erant, inquit, in monte mo- nasteria tanquam tabernacula; » et Rufinus refert (Lib.iide Vit. Pat., c. 23) fratres congregatos « sub una die monasterium construxisse. » Quod de coeno- bio quis credat? Et ibidem cuidam saeculo nuntium remittere cupienti, et requirenti ab abbate Ammonio cellulam vacantem : « Tunc ille, inquit : Ego inqui- ram, sed donec inveniam hic esto in hoc monaste- rio,....
passages.english: And indeed it is established that the word "monastery" is frequently used in the Lives of the holy Fathers to designate the dwelling of a single monk. Hence St Athanasius in the Life of St Antony (ch. 21): "There were," he says, "monasteries on the mountain like tents"; and Rufinus reports (Book 2 of the Lives of the Fathers, ch. 23) that the brothers, having gathered, "built a monastery in one day." Who would believe this of a cenobium? And in the same place, of a certain man who wished to renounce the world and asked Abbot Ammonius for a vacant cell: "Then he said: I will look, but until I find [one], stay here in this monastery,....
passages.notes: The stray "42" is a page number and has been omitted. "Lib.iide" has been read as "Lib. II de."

passages.original: Hieronymus et Cassianus, et quorum in Veteri Testamento Elias et Elisaeus, in Novo autem Testamento Joannes Baptista aliquas nobis exhibue- runt umbras, « hi sunt qui habitant per deserta, » inquit S. Hieronymus (Epist. 22); sive, ut ait apud Cassianum abbas Piamon (Collat. 18, cap. 4), qui « prius in coenobiis instituti, jamque actuali conver- satione perfecti, solitudinis elegere secreta; » qui « nequaquam contenti hac victoria qua inter homi- nes occultas insidias diaboli conculcaverunt, aperto certamine ac manifesto conflictu daemonibus con- gredi cupientes, vastos eremi recessus penetrare non timent;
passages.english: [the] anchorites, whose leaders St Jerome and Cassian made Paul and Antony, and of whom in the Old Testament Elijah and Elisha, and in the New Testament John the Baptist, have shown us some foreshadowings: "these are those who dwell in the deserts," says St Jerome (Epist. 22); or, as Abbot Piamun says in Cassian (Conference 18, ch. 4), those who, "first trained in cenobia and now perfected in the active life, have chosen the seclusion of solitude"; who, "by no means content with that victory by which they have trampled down the hidden snares of the devil among men, desiring to engage the demons in open combat and manifest conflict, do not fear to penetrate the vast recesses of the desert;

passages.original: Sed monasterii probatione diuturna.] Hoc nimirum exigebat priscorum monachorum disciplina, ut in eremo non admitterent, nisi diu probatos in coeno- bio : « De ludo monasteriorum hujusmodi volumus, egredi milites, quos eremi dura rudimenta non ter- reant, » inquit S. Hieronymus ad Rusticum mona- chum scribens (Epist. 4). Idem docet apud Cassia- num abbas Piamon supra citatus. Idem statutum le- gitur in concilio Veneto anno 465, can. 7; in conci- lio Toletano vii, can. 5; in sexta synodo canone 41. Idem videre est in Vita S.
passages.english: But by long testing in the monastery.] This indeed the discipline of the ancient monks required: that they not admit [anyone] to the desert except those long tested in the cenobium. "From the training-school of monasteries of this kind we want soldiers to go forth whom the hard first lessons of the desert do not frighten," says St Jerome writing to Rusticus the monk (Epist. 4). Abbot Piamun, cited above, teaches the same in Cassian. The same is found decreed in the Council of Vannes in the year 465, canon 7; in the Seventh Council of Toledo, canon 5; and in the Sixth Synod, canon 41. The same may be seen in the Life of St
passages.notes: "Concilio Veneto" has been taken as the Council of Vannes.

passages.original: Theodosius Coenobiarcha (In ejus Vit. cap. 2; Boll. 11 jan.). Adde quod anachoresis in jugi rerum coelestium contemplatione consistit, ad quam, nisi praevia in coenobiis activa vita, perveniri non potest, ut docet inter alios apud Cassianum abbas Nesteros collat. 14, c. 2; et in Regula Solitariorum Grimlaicus his verbis : « Ad fastigium contempla- tivae vitae quisquis conatur ascendere, semetipsum debet prius per multa experimenta in activa vita probare.
passages.english: Theodosius the Coenobiarch (in his Life, ch. 2; Bollandists, 11 January). Add that anchoritism consists in the unbroken contemplation of heavenly things, which cannot be reached except by a preceding active life in cenobia, as Abbot Nesteros teaches, among others, in Cassian (Conference 14, ch. 2), and Grimlaic in the Rule for Solitaries in these words: "Whoever strives to ascend to the summit of the contemplative life must first prove himself through many trials in the active life.

passages.original: » Et iterum rationem reddens : « Qui morbis animi laborat, et tamen vi- tam solitariam audet aggredi, perinde facit ac qui in alto mari ex navi desilit in fluctus, et in tabula exi- stimat se sine periculo in portum evasurum; » et quia, ut ait Cassianus, solitudo « eorum qui minus emen- dati sunt, vitia non solum servare, verum etiam exaggerare consuevit. » Sed de his satis.
passages.english: And again, giving the reason: "He who suffers from diseases of the soul and yet dares to undertake the solitary life acts just like one who on the high sea leaps from the ship into the waves and thinks that on a plank he will escape into harbour without danger"; and because, as Cassian says, solitude "is accustomed not only to preserve but even to increase the vices of those who are less amended." But enough of these things.

passages.original: Be- nedictus, unde et illud vocat teterrimum, id est « ni- gerrimum, obscurissimum, horribile, agreste, vel ferum, » inquit Smaragdus. Eodem modo S. Hiero- nymus (Epist. 22) : « Tertium genus est quod Re- mohoth dicunt teterrimum atque neglectum. » Et apud Cassianum abbas Piamon (Collat. 18, cap. 7): « Emersit post haec illud teterrimum et infidele mona- chorum genus, vel potius 49 noxia illa plantatio re- diviva concrevit, quae per Ananiam et Saphiram in exordio Ecclesiae apostoli Petri severitate succisa est. » Ubi quod ait ab Anania et Saphira originem duxisse, idem asserunt S. Isidorus lib. ii de Eccles.
passages.english: Benedict, whence he also calls it "teterrimum", that is, "most black, most obscure, horrible, rustic, or savage," says Smaragdus. In the same way St Jerome (Epist. 22): "The third kind is that which they call Remnuoth, most foul and neglected." And Abbot Piamun in Cassian (Conference 18, ch. 7): "After these there arose that most foul and faithless kind of monks, or rather that harmful plant grew up again revived, which at the beginning of the Church was cut down by the severity of the apostle Peter in Ananias and Sapphira." As to his saying that it took its origin from Ananias and Sapphira, St Isidore asserts the same in Book 2 of On Ecclesiastical
passages.notes: The edition prints "Remohoth"; Jerome's form is usually Remnuoth. The stray "49" is a page number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Mentiri Deo per tonsuram noscuntur.] Quia, ut di- cit apud Cassianum abbas Piamon, « ad publicum tantummodo, id est ad hominum faciem renuntiantes, aut in suis domiciliis sub privilegio hujus nominis (scilicet monachi) iisdem obstricti occupationibus perseverant, 50 aut construentes sibi cellulas, casque monasteria nuncupantes, suo in eis jure ac libertate consistunt, nequaquam evangelicis praecep- tionibus succumbentes, ut nulli scilicet quotidiani victus sollicitudine, nullis rei familiaris distentioni- bus occupentur.
passages.english: They are known to lie to God by their tonsure.] Because, as Abbot Piamun says in Cassian, "renouncing only publicly, that is, before the eyes of men, they either continue in their own homes, under the privilege of this name (namely, 'monk'), bound by the same occupations, or, building cells for themselves and calling them monasteries, they remain in them under their own right and freedom, by no means submitting to the precepts of the Gospel, namely, that they be occupied with no anxiety for daily food and no distractions of household affairs.
passages.notes: "Casque" has been read as "easque." The stray "50" is a page number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Qui bini aut terni aut certe singuli.] Similiter S. Hieronymus (Epist. 22) : « Hi bini, vel terni, nec multo plures simul habitant; » et apud Cassianum abbas Piamon : « Illi autem qui districtionem, ut diximus, declinantes, bini vel terni in cellulis com- morantur, » etc. : in hoc aliquam anachoreticae et coenobiticae vitae speciem prae se ferentes, neutram autem in rei veritate tenentes : non primam, propter societatem, quam respuit anachoresis;
passages.english: Who [live] two or three together, or even singly.] Similarly St Jerome (Letter 22): "These live two or three together, and not many more at once"; and in Cassian the abbot Piamon [says]: "But those who, as we have said, avoid the strictness [of discipline] and dwell two or three together in cells," etc.: in this they display some appearance of both the anachoretic and the cenobitic life, but in truth hold to neither: not the first, because of the companionship, which the anchoritic life rejects;
passages.notes: Anachoresis/anachoretic = the hermit's life; cenobitic = communal monastic life.

passages.original: Ipsi denique in Aegypto erant in foraminibus petra- rum habitantes, induti porcorum et boum pellibus, tantum cincti funibus, palmarum spinas ad calcaria portantes ad cingulum ligatas, discalceati et san- guine cruentati, cavernas exeuntes ad festum Coeno- paegiae pergebant Hierosolymam, et Sancta sancio- rum intrantes paupertatem et abstinentiam praedica- bant animi affectu servare : barbas postmodum in conspectu hominum sine redemptione evellere festi- nabant, et sic acquisita fama et lucro, ad propria remeabant, solitarie gaudentes, et epulantes supra id quod explicare possumus. » Sane nullum tunc tem- poris erat Hierosolymis templum Judaeorum, nec aliquid horum reperitur apud Hieronymum aut Cas- sianum qui sarabaitarum mores satis accurate de- scripserunt. Idem tamen pene de verbo ad verbum videre est in antiquis Lectionibus Celii Rhodigini lib. xxvii, cap. 6.
passages.english: "They in Egypt, then, lived in holes in the rocks, clothed in the skins of pigs and oxen, girded only with ropes, carrying palm thorns tied to their belts for spurs, barefoot and stained with blood; leaving their caves they went to Jerusalem for the feast of Coenopegia, and entering the Holy of Holies they proclaimed that they kept poverty and abstinence with the disposition of the mind; afterwards they hastened to pluck out their beards in the sight of men without ransom, and so, having gained fame and profit, they returned to their own homes, rejoicing in solitude and feasting beyond what we can describe." Certainly at that time there was no temple of the Jews at Jerusalem, nor is anything of this found in Jerome or Cassian, who described the habits of the sarabaites quite accurately. Yet the same thing can be seen almost word for word in the Antique Readings of Caelius Rhodiginus, book 27, chapter 6.
passages.notes: Coenopegia (Coenopaegia) = Greek name for the Feast of Tabernacles. "Sine redemptione" (without ransom/redemption) is obscure in sense. "Sancioru" read as sanctorum.

passages.original: Pro lege eis est desideriorum voluptas.] Ideo pasto- rem habere refugiunt, ut liberius quod libuerit im- pleant, « non contenti abbatis cura atque imperio gubernari, inquit apud Cassianum abbas Piamon, sed hoc praecipue procurantes, ut absoluti a senio- rum jugo, exercendi voluntates suas, et procedendi, vel quo placuerit evagandi, agendive quod libitum fuerit habeant libertatem. » Ex quo sequitur quod ait S. Hieronymus : « Inter hos saepe sunt jurgia, quia suo viventes cibo non patiuntur se alicui esse subje- ctos : revera solent certare jejuniis, et rem secreti victoriae faciunt. Apud hos affectata sunt omnia, laxae manicae, caligae follicantes, vestis crassior, cre- bra suspiria, visitatio virginum, detractio clerico- rum, et si quando dies festus venerit, saturantur usque ad vomitum. »
passages.english: The pleasure of their desires is their law.] They shun having a shepherd precisely so that they may more freely do whatever they please, "not content," says the abbot Piamon in Cassian, "to be governed by the care and command of an abbot, but taking care above all that, released from the yoke of the elders, they may have freedom to exercise their own wills, to go out or wander wherever they please, and to do whatever they like." From this follows what St Jerome says: "Among these there are often quarrels, because, living on their own food, they do not allow themselves to be subject to anyone; indeed they are accustomed to compete in fasting, and make a matter of secrecy into an occasion of victory. With them everything is affected: loose sleeves, baggy boots, coarser clothing, frequent sighs, visiting of virgins, disparagement of clerics; and whenever a feast day comes, they gorge themselves to the point of vomiting."
passages.notes: "rem secreti victoriae faciunt": sense somewhat uncertain—they turn what should be private into a contest.

passages.original: Benedictus ait quidquid elegerint, non quidquid eis praecipitur : in quo iterum discrepant a coenobitis, quorum est alieno parere imperio; non quod placuerit eligere. Sed miseri non advertunt quod ait abbas Piamon apud Cassianum : Hos arbi- trii sui tepor vivos ad inferna demergit.
passages.english: Benedict says "whatever they have chosen," not "whatever is commanded them": in this again they differ from cenobites, whose part is to obey another's command, not to choose what pleases them. But the wretches do not notice what the abbot Piamon says in Cassian: The lukewarmness of their own choice plunges them alive into hell.

passages.original: Propriam coenobita non sequitur volun- tatem, sed ad illius exemplum qui pro nobis factus est obediens usque ad mortem, humiliter abbati sub- jectus in omnibus obtemperat : at vero eremita cum supra se neminem habeat cui subjiciatur, neminem imperantem cui obsequatur, obedientiae merito pri- vatur. Quas quidem duas rationes tanti faciebat abbas Joannes, ut eas omnibus deserti utilitatibus antefer- ret, uti ipse testatur apud Cassianum ( Collat. 19, cap. 6) sic loquens : « Si mihi in coenobio constituto ab illa puritate cordis aliquid fuerit imminutum, 57 ero solius evangelici praecepti compensatione conten- tus, quod certum est omnibus illis eremi fructibus non posse postponi, ut scilicet de crastino nihil cogitem, et usque ad finem subjectus abbati illum aliquatenus videar aemulari de quo dicitur: Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens usque ad mortem, me- rearque illius verbum humiliter dicere, quia non veni facere voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me Patris.
passages.english: The cenobite does not follow his own will, but, after the example of him who for us became obedient unto death, humbly subject to the abbot, he obeys in all things; whereas the hermit, since he has no one above him to whom he is subject, no one commanding whom he obeys, is deprived of the merit of obedience. Abbot John valued these two reasons so highly that he preferred them to all the advantages of the desert, as he himself testifies in Cassian (Conference 19, chapter 6), speaking thus: "If, when I am placed in a monastery, something of that purity of heart is diminished, I shall be content with the compensation of the gospel precept alone, which certainly cannot be ranked below all those fruits of the desert: namely, that I take no thought for the morrow, and, subject to the abbot until the end, may seem in some measure to imitate him of whom it is said: He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death; and that I may deserve humbly to say his words: For I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.
passages.notes: The number 57 in the text is a page marker, omitted.

passages.original: Duodecimo. Tandem copiosior in coelo merces coenobitae servatur, ut discimus ex visione cujusdam Patris, quam refert Rufinus his verbis (Lib.iiide Vit. Pat. n. 141): « Quidam ex Patribus in exstasi positus vidit quatuor ordines ante Deum; et primus quidem erat hominum infirmantium, et gratias agen- tium Deo; secundus vero erat eorum qui hospitali- tatem sectantur, et in hoc stant et ministrant;
passages.english: Twelfth. Finally, a more abundant reward in heaven is reserved for the cenobite, as we learn from the vision of a certain Father, which Rufinus relates in these words (Lives of the Fathers, book 3, no. 141): "One of the Fathers, placed in ecstasy, saw four orders before God; and the first was of men who were sick and giving thanks to God; the second was of those who pursue hospitality, and stand firm in this and serve;

passages.original: His atque aliis hujusmodi rationibus convicti asceticae vitae magistri, anachoresi non modo non inferiorem, sed et longe utiliorem vitam coenobiticam praedicarunt; unde et abbas Joannes apud Cassianum (Coll. 19, c. 3) cum viginti annos in solitudine exe- gisset, ad coenobium libens et gaudens reversus est: S. P. Benedictus et multi alii ab anachoresi incoepe- runt, 60 in coenobio vitae finem fecerunt;
passages.english: Convinced by these and other reasons of this kind, the masters of the ascetic life proclaimed the cenobitic life to be not only not inferior to the anchoritic, but even far more useful; hence also abbot John, in Cassian (Conference 19, chapter 3), after he had spent twenty years in solitude, returned willingly and joyfully to the monastery; our holy Father Benedict and many others began from the anchoritic life [and] ended their life in the monastery;
passages.notes: The number 60 is a page marker, omitted.

passages.original: Ber- nardus ad Balduinum abbatem scribens (Epist. 201): « In his duobus mandatis, inquit, verbi scilicet et exempli summam tui officii ac conscientiae securita- tem pendere intellige. » Et certe, ut optime arguit S. Hieronymus : « Sancta rusticitas solum sibi prod- est; et quantum aedificat exemplo et vitae merito Ecclesiam Christi, tantum nocet, si destruentibus non resistat; et innocens absque sermone conversatio, quantum exemplo prodest, tantum silentio nocet; nam latratu canum, et baculo pastorum deterrenda est rabies luporum. » Et econtra « nihil est turpius quam si bonum quod quisque praedicat, explere opere negligat, » inquit S. Isidorus (Lib.iiide Sum. Bono, c. 36). Quapropter apud Rufinum abbas Poemen di- cebat (Lib.iiide Vit. Pat. n. 185): « Homo qui alios docet, et non facit ca quae docet, similis est fonti alto, qui omnium res lavat, et omnes saliat potu, seipsum autem lavare non potest, sed habet et im- munditias, et sordes limorum.
passages.english: Bernard, writing to Abbot Baldwin (Letter 201), says: "Understand that in these two commands, namely of word and of example, hang the sum of your office and the security of your conscience." And certainly, as St Jerome argues excellently: "Holy rusticity benefits only itself; and as much as it builds up the Church of Christ by example and the merit of its life, so much it harms if it does not resist those who tear down; and an innocent way of life without speech does as much harm by its silence as it does good by its example; for the fury of wolves must be deterred by the barking of dogs and the staff of shepherds." And conversely, "nothing is more shameful than if someone neglects to fulfil in deed the good that he preaches," says St Isidore (On the Highest Good, book 3, chapter 36). Therefore in Rufinus the abbot Poemen used to say (Lives of the Fathers, book 3, no. 185): "A man who teaches others and does not do what he teaches is like a deep spring, which washes everyone's things and satisfies all with drink, but cannot wash itself, and has impurities and the filth of mud.
passages.notes: "ca" read as "ea"; "saliat" read as "satiat".

passages.original: 27), « abundant qui malae suae vitae defensionem ex ipsis suis praepositis et doctoribus quaerunt, respondentes corde suo, aut etiam si ad hoc erumpant ore suo, atque dicentes : Quod mihi praecipis cur ipse non facis? Ita fit ut eum non obedienter audiant, qui se ipse non audit, et Dei verbum, quod eis prae- dicatur, simul cum ipso praedicatore contemnunt. » Hinc S. Hieronymus ad Nepotianum scribens : « Non confundant, inquit, opera sermonem tuum, ne cum in ecclesia loqueris, tacitus quisque respondeat : Cur haec quae dicis ipse non facis? » Concinit Cassianus in libro de Spiritu irae (Lib.viiiInstit., cap. 5), ubi sic loquitur. « Oportet illum qui alterius vulneri mederi cupit, omni languoris morbo alienum sanum- que subsistere, ne il ud evangelicum dicatur ei : Medice, prius cura teipsum, ac videns festucam in oculo fratris sui, trabem in oculo suo non videat.
passages.english: 27), "there are many who seek a defence of their bad life from their own superiors and teachers, answering in their heart, or even, if they break out into it, with their mouth, and saying: Why do you not yourself do what you command me? So it happens that they do not listen obediently to one who does not listen to himself, and they despise the word of God that is preached to them together with the preacher himself." Hence St Jerome, writing to Nepotian, says: "Let your deeds not confound your words, lest when you speak in church each person silently answers: Why do you not yourself do these things you say?" Cassian agrees in his book on the spirit of anger (Institutes, book 8, chapter 5), where he speaks thus: "He who wishes to heal another's wound must remain sound and free from every disease of sickness, lest that gospel word be said to him: Physician, first heal yourself, and [lest], seeing the speck in his brother's eye, he not see the beam in his own eye.

passages.original: sive, ut habet in secundo, « an sit parvus et magnus, senex vel juve- nis, vicinus vel advena, clericus vel laicus; » Christi enim vices in monasterio agere creditur, apud quem non est personarum acceptio, sed in omni gente in iis qui timent illum, acceptum est illi. Hinc S. Ja- cobus apostolus in Epistola (Cap.ii) ait : « Fratres, nolite in personarum acceptione habere fidem Domi- ni nostri Jesu Christi gloriae; etenim si introierit in conventum vestrum vir aureum annulum habens in veste candida, introierit autem pauper in sordido ha- bitu; et intendatis in eum qui indutus est veste prae- clara, et dixeritis ei : Tu sede hic bene; pauperi autem dicatis : Tu sta illic, aut sede sub scabello pedum meorum; nonne judicatis apud vosmetipsos, et facti estis judices cogitationum noxiarum? » Quod quantum sit malum, indicat S. Ambrosius super Malachiam scribens in haec verba : « Inter omnia pec- cata sacerdotum maximum est, quod non causas, sed personas considerant, et despecto justo paupere, injustos divites honorant. » Ex quibus liquet quam merito jure S.
passages.english: or, as he has it in the second, "whether he be small or great, old or young, neighbour or stranger, cleric or layman"; for he is believed to act in Christ's place in the monastery, with whom there is no respect of persons, but in every nation those who fear him are acceptable to him. Hence St James the apostle says in his Epistle (chapter 2): "Brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with respect of persons; for if a man with a gold ring, in white clothing, comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in, and you pay attention to the one wearing splendid clothing and say to him: Sit here in a good place; but say to the poor man: Stand there, or sit under my footstool; do you not judge among yourselves, and have you not become judges with evil thoughts?" How great an evil this is St Ambrose indicates, writing on Malachi in these words: "Among all the sins of priests the greatest is that they consider not causes but persons, and, despising the just poor man, honour the unjust rich." From this it is clear how rightly St
passages.notes: "in the second" presumably refers to a second commentator or version; referent unclear from the passage. "quam merito jure" doubled adverbs rendered as "how rightly".

passages.original: Apud Deum anima uniuscujusque 78 non est discernenda nobilitate, sed opere; nec genere, sed actione.» Et S. Gregorii Lib.iReg. cap. 72): « Apud Deum non gradus ele- gantior, sed vitae melioris actio comprobatur. » Unde et Aristoteles dicebat (I Polit.) : « virtus et malitia determinant servos et liberos, nobiles et ignobiles. » Porro S. Benedictus bonis operibus humilitatem adjungit; quia, ut apprime scribit S. Gregorius, « qui sine humilitate virtutes congre- gat, quasi in ventum pulverem portat;
passages.english: "With God the soul of each person is to be distinguished not by nobility but by work, not by birth but by action." And [that] of St. Gregory, Book 1 of the Register, chapter 72: "With God it is not the more elegant rank but the action of a better life that is approved." Hence Aristotle too said (Politics 1): "Virtue and vice determine slaves and free, noble and ignoble." Further, St. Benedict joins humility to good works, because, as St. Gregory writes most aptly, "he who gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind;
passages.notes: The numeral "78" in the text is a page or marginal number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: Una praebeatur omnibus secundum merita disciplina.] Id est correctio sive punitio, ubi nimirum eadem est culpa, juxta illud S. Hieronymi : « Nullius accipias personam, non divitias, non potentias; quantum- cunque sit potens, vel nobilis, si peccaverit, corripe eum, et comedisti azyma sinceritatis in amaritu- dine. » Plane usque adeo exosa fuit priscis Patribus in correptionibus et judiciis ferendis personarum acceptio, ut negligentem hac in re praepositum, et ju- dicantem non secundum rei veritatem, sed secun- dum personas, de solio deponi praecipiat S.
passages.english: Let one discipline be applied to all according to their merits.] That is, correction or punishment, namely where the fault is the same, according to that saying of St. Jerome: "Respect no one's person, not riches, not powers; however powerful or noble he may be, if he has sinned, rebuke him, and you have eaten the unleavened bread of sincerity with bitterness." Indeed, respect of persons in giving corrections and judgements was so hateful to the ancient Fathers that St.
passages.notes: The sentence continues into the following context: St. Pachomius (Rule, art. 94) orders that a superior who is negligent in this matter, and who judges not according to the truth of the case but according to persons, be deposed from his seat until he amends.

passages.original: Apostolicam illam debet semper formam servare, in qua dicit : Argue, obsecra, increpa.] Quae verba sic ex- plicat citatus a Smaragdo S. Hieronymus : Argue peccantes, contestare ne peccent, increpa resisten- tes; et S. Prosper : Argue coaequales, obsecra senio- res, increpa juniores; Richardus de S. Angelo : Ar- gue admonendo, obsecra comminando, increpa ad poenam procedendo. At omnium optimam, ut existi- mat Smaragdus, apostolicae sententiae expositionem tradit S.
passages.english: He must always keep that apostolic form in which he says: Reprove, entreat, rebuke.] These words St. Jerome, cited by Smaragdus, explains thus: Reprove those who sin, warn them not to sin, rebuke those who resist. And St. Prosper: Reprove your equals, entreat your elders, rebuke the younger. Richard of Sant'Angelo: Reprove by admonishing, entreat by threatening, rebuke by proceeding to punishment. But the best exposition of all of the apostolic saying, as Smaragdus judges, is given by St.
passages.notes: The sentence is completed in the following context: "Benedict, when he adds:".

passages.original: Porro ex hac bonorum et improborum in corre- ctionibus discretione, colliges non locis sanctificari homines, sed hominibus loca; nullamque exstars tam sanctam congregationem, quae suo in sinu malos aliquos non complectatur, ut egregie docet apud Cassianum abbas Piamon (Coll. 18, c. 16) : « Nec perversos, inquit, atque exsecrabiles quosque san- ctorum virorum numero insertos latitare miremur; quin dum in hujus saeculi area conculcamur atque conterimur, necesse est etiam paleas igni perpetuo deputandas inter electissima frumenta misceri. De- nique si vel Satan inter angelos, vel Judam inter apostolos, vel Nicolaum pravissimae haereseos inven- torem inter diaconos reminiscamur electos, hoc quod nequissimi homines sanctorum ordini depre- henduntur inserti, mirum esse non poterit.
passages.english: Further, from this distinction between the good and the wicked in corrections, you will gather that men are not sanctified by places, but places by men; and that there exists no congregation so holy that it does not hold some wicked men in its bosom, as Abbot Piamun excellently teaches in Cassian (Conference 18, ch. 16): "Nor should we wonder," he says, "that perverse and execrable people lie hidden, inserted among the number of holy men; for while we are trodden and threshed on the threshing-floor of this world, it is necessary that chaff destined for the everlasting fire be mixed even among the choicest grain. Finally, if we remember that Satan was chosen among the angels, or Judas among the apostles, or Nicolas, the inventor of a most depraved heresy, among the deacons, it cannot be a wonder that most wicked men are found inserted in the order of the saints.
passages.notes: "exstars" read as "exstare".

passages.original: Et dicat ipse unde agitur.] Convocatis fratribus, abbas rem cujus causa congregavit eos, exponit; quia, ut ait Plato (In Phaedro), « in omni re consu- lendi principium, nosse id de quo consilium institu- tum; aut tota via aberrare necessum est. » Antequam vero tractandum negotium exponat, ex Hildemaro, « oculis corporeis fixis in terra, et oculo cordis in Deum, rogare debet Deum dicens: Domine, rogo cle- mentiam tuam, ut per quem vis manifestare, dignare indicare.» Divino implorato auxilio, negotium expli- cet, allatis utrinque rationibus, sic tamen ut suam ipse non aperiat sententiam, ut omnis tollatur adu- lationi aut assentationi occasio, ut libera et integra etiam timidioribus quid sentiant exponendi licentia detur, et ne forte inveniatur male feriatus aliquis, maligno discordiae spiritu agitatus, qui ut aliquam procreet abbati molestiam, cognito ejus desiderio, in contrariam abeat sententiam.
passages.english: And let him himself state what is at issue.] When the brothers have been called together, the abbot sets out the matter for which he has assembled them; because, as Plato says (in the Phaedrus), "in every matter the beginning of deliberating is to know that about which the deliberation has been undertaken; otherwise one must go astray along the whole way." But before he sets out the business to be discussed, according to Hildemar, "with his bodily eyes fixed on the ground and the eye of his heart on God, he ought to ask God, saying: Lord, I beg your mercy, that you may deign to show through whom you wish to make [it] manifest." Having implored divine help, let him explain the business, bringing forward reasons on both sides, yet in such a way that he does not reveal his own opinion, so that every occasion for flattery or assent may be removed, so that free and full liberty to state what they think may be given even to the more timid, and lest perhaps someone ill-disposed be found, stirred by the malign spirit of discord, who, in order to cause the abbot some trouble, once he knows his wish, goes over to the contrary opinion.
passages.notes: "male feriatus" (literally 'idle in a bad way') rendered as 'ill-disposed'.

passages.original: Hinc Paulus apostolus, Si ju- niori, inquit, revelatum fuerit, senior taceat (I Cor.xiv). Quia ergo juniori saepe Dominus revelat quod melius est, juniores etiam novissimos ad consilium vocari voluit S. Benedictus; qua etiam ratione eos veteres monachi in suis collationibus, ut testatur Cassianus (Collat. 16, c. 12), admittebant : quamvis in nonnullis monachorum congregationibus soli sa- cris ordinibus initiati, ut minimum subdiaconi, ca- pitularibus tractationibus intersint. Atque ita apud Carthusianos ex nova collectione statutorum, ii parte, cap.
passages.english: Hence the apostle Paul says: If something has been revealed to a younger one, let the elder be silent (1 Cor. 14). Since, therefore, the Lord often reveals to the younger what is better, St. Benedict wished even the youngest juniors to be called to counsel; for which reason also the ancient monks admitted them to their conferences, as Cassian testifies (Conference 16, ch. 12): although in some congregations of monks only those initiated into sacred orders, at least subdeacons, take part in chapter deliberations. And so it is among the Carthusians according to the new collection of statutes, part 2, chapter
passages.notes: The paraphrase of 1 Cor. 14 is loose. The chapter number (4) falls in the following context.

passages.original: Ipse tamen abbas cum timore Dei et observatione regulae omnia faciat.] Primo cum timore Dei, quia, ut dicit citatus a Boherio Cassiodorus, « semper bene geritur, si coelestis metus humanis moribus appona- tur. » Deinde cum observatione regulae, ut ostende- ret non minus abbatem quam monachos regulae subdi.
passages.english: Yet let the abbot himself do everything with the fear of God and observance of the rule.] First, with the fear of God, because, as Cassiodorus, cited by Boherius, says, "things are always done well if heavenly fear is applied to human conduct." Next, with observance of the rule, to show that the abbot is no less subject to the rule than the monks.

passages.original: Imprimis Dominum Deum diligire ex toto corde, tota anima; tota virtute.] Primum inquit instrumentum diligere Deum, hoc est enim primum et maximum in lege mandatum : primum dignitate, primum utili- tate, primum necessitate. Dignitate, quia, ut dicit apud Cassianum (Collat. 11, c. 12) abbas Chaeremon, « nihil pretiosius, nihil perfectius, nihil sublimius, nihil charitate perennius; » et Sanctus Caesarius (Serm. 107 in Append. Serm. S. Aug.): « Charitas oleo comparatur;
passages.english: First of all, to love the Lord God with the whole heart, the whole soul, the whole strength.] He says that the first instrument is to love God, for this is the first and greatest commandment in the law: first in dignity, first in usefulness, first in necessity. In dignity, because, as Abbot Chaeremon says in Cassian (Conference 11, ch. 12), "nothing is more precious, nothing more perfect, nothing more sublime, nothing more lasting than charity"; and St. Caesarius (Sermon 107 in the Appendix of the Sermons of St. Augustine): "Charity is compared to oil;
passages.notes: "diligire" read as "diligere".

passages.original: Non adulterari.] Adulterii nomine omne fornica- tionis genus prohibet, non solum carnalis, sed etiam spiritualis; cujus quinque species apud Cassianum (Collat. 14, cap. 11) enumerat abbas Nesteros, sci- licet: 1. Idololatriam, de qua apud Jeremiam argui- tur Jerusalem, quod fornicata sit in omni colle su- blimi, et sub omni ligno frondoso. 2. Omnem gen- tilium superstitionem in auguriis et observationibus dierum et temporum. 3. Superstitiones Judaicas in caeremoniis legalibus. 4. Haeresim. 5. « Quae in co- gitationum pervagatione consistit: quia omnis cogi- tatio non solum turpis, sed etiam otiosa, et a Deo quantulumcunque discedens, a perfecto viro immun- dissima fornicatio deputatur.
passages.english: Not to commit adultery.] Under the name of adultery he forbids every kind of fornication, not only carnal but also spiritual, of which Abbot Nesteros in Cassian (Conference 14, ch. 11) lists five species, namely: 1. Idolatry, for which Jerusalem is reproved in Jeremiah, because she fornicated on every high hill and under every leafy tree. 2. Every superstition of the gentiles in auguries and observances of days and seasons. 3. Jewish superstitions in the ceremonies of the law. 4. Heresy. 5. "That which consists in the wandering of the thoughts: because every thought, not only shameful but even idle, and departing from God however little, is reckoned by the perfect man a most impure fornication.

passages.original: et iterum alii sunt qui sine fructu, quia inviti, et cum murmure jejunant : sed quod perfectum est, jejunium amare, et quidem non solum carnis, sed quod majus est, cordis. « Opor- tet enim, ut ait Cassianus, exteriore homine jeju- nante, interiorem quoque similiter a cibis noxiis temperare. » Sed quia tunc vere jejunamus cum ea quae subtrahimus corpori, pauperum cedimus refe- ctioni, apte omnino S.
passages.english: and again there are others who fast without fruit, because unwillingly and with grumbling; but what is perfect is to love fasting, and indeed not only of the flesh but, what is greater, of the heart. "For," as Cassian says, "while the outer man fasts, the inner man too must likewise abstain from harmful foods." But because we truly fast when we give up for the refreshment of the poor what we withdraw from the body, St.
passages.notes: The sentence is completed in the following context: "Benedict quite fittingly adds:".

passages.original: Quam profusi fuerint in re- creandis pauperibus veteres monachi, nec lingua di- cere, nec intellectus capere potest. Praesertim vero non sine aliquo animi stupore legere valemus quod de egregiis illis sub Serapione abbate militantibus Christo refert Rufinus (Lib.iide Vit. Pat., c. 18. Idem scribit Pallad. in Laus., c. 76) : « Hoc autem, inquit, moris erat non solum ipsis, sed et omnibus pene AEgyptiis monachis, ut messis tempore elocent ad metendum operam suam, atque ex ea mercede octog nos unusquisque modios frumenti plus minus conquireret, et horum partem plurimam pauperum usibus offerant; unde non solum regionis ipsius indi- gentes alantur, sed et Alexandriam naves frumento onustae dirigantur, vel in carcere conclusis, vel reli- quis peregrinis, atque egentibus prorogandae.
passages.english: How lavish the monks of old were in relieving the poor, no tongue can tell nor understanding grasp. Above all, we cannot read without some astonishment what Rufinus relates (Book II of the Lives of the Fathers, ch. 18; Palladius writes the same in the Lausiac History, ch. 76) about those excellent men who served as soldiers of Christ under the abbot Serapion: "This was the custom," he says, "not only among them but among nearly all the monks of Egypt: at harvest time they hire out their labour for reaping, and from that wage each of them would acquire about eighty measures of grain, more or less, and they offer the greater part of these for the use of the poor; so that not only are the needy of that region itself fed, but ships laden with grain are also sent to Alexandria, to be distributed either to those shut up in prison or to other strangers and the needy.
passages.notes: 'octog nos' read as 'octogenos' (eighty each); 'elocent' as 'elocent/locent' (hire out). 'modios' rendered 'measures' (modii).

passages.original: Iram non perficere.] Quod ait iram non perficere, ostendit varios esse gradus irae, quos recensent Cas- sianus collatione 5, cap. 11, et Joannes Climacus gradu 8. Plura etiam de ira disputat idem Cassianus iu libro viii de Spiritu irae, quem vide, si lubet. Quo- modo etiam fieri possit, ut non irascatur monachus, docet S. Basilius in brevibus Regulis interrogatione 2. Plura de ira dicere supersedemus, cum raro videas monachos in schola humilitatis huic vitio subjacere.
passages.english: Not to carry out anger.] In saying "not to carry out anger" he shows that there are various degrees of anger, which Cassian lists in Conference 5, ch. 11, and John Climacus in Step 8. The same Cassian also discusses anger at greater length in Book VIII, On the Spirit of Anger, which see, if you like. How it may come about that a monk is not angry, St Basil teaches in the Shorter Rules, question 2. We refrain from saying more about anger, since you rarely see monks in the school of humility subject to this vice.
passages.notes: 'iu' read as 'in'.

passages.original: Charitatem non derelinquere.] Quid sit charitas, docet S. Augustinum cum dicit (Lib.iiide Doctr. Christ. cap. 10): « Charitatem voco motum a imi?ad fruendum Deo propter ipsum, et se atque proximo propter Deum. » Porro qui charitatem derelinquit, Deum ipsum amittit, quia Deus charitas est, et qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo.
passages.english: Not to forsake charity.] What charity is, St Augustine teaches when he says (Book III of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 10): "I call charity the motion of the soul towards enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one's neighbour for God's sake." Moreover, whoever forsakes charity loses God himself, because God is charity, and whoever abides in charity abides in God, and God in him.
passages.notes: 'Augustinum' read as 'Augustinus'; 'a imi?' as 'animi'; 'proximo' as 'proximo/proximum'.

passages.original: Verum hoc praeser- tim instrumento mendacium interdicitur, quod nun- quam fuit, nec erit aliquando licitum; quamvis con- trarium censuerint Plato lib iii de Repub., hac in re plane non divinus; Origenes lib. vi Stromatum, et apud Cassianum abbas Joseph collat. 17. cap. 17; quorum doctrinae refragantur S. Augustinus in lib. de Mendacio, et in lib. Contra Mendac.; S. Thomas, 2-2, q. 110, a. 3, et multi alii. Et certe ita exosa fuit abbatis Josephi sententia, ut hanc ob rem aliosque errores Cassiani collationem 17 censura affecerit olim Facultas theologica Parisiensis, ut ex veteri ms.
passages.english: But by this instrument above all lying is forbidden, which never has been nor ever will be lawful; although the contrary was held by Plato in Book III of the Republic, plainly not divine in this matter; by Origen in Book VI of the Stromata; and, in Cassian, by abbot Joseph, Conference 17, ch. 17. Against their teaching stand St Augustine in the book On Lying and in the book Against Lying; St Thomas, II-II, q. 110, a. 3; and many others. And indeed the opinion of abbot Joseph was so detested that for this reason and for other errors the Theological Faculty of Paris once laid a censure on Cassian's Conference 17, as from an old manuscript
passages.notes: Sentence continues into the following context ('...Alard Gazet observes').

passages.original: 131Malum pro malo non reddere.] Quia, ut cita- tus ab Hildemaro Origenes ait : « Pejor est ille qui vicem reddit, quam ille qui malum in primis facit. » Hoc instrumentum perfecte implevit S. Hugo abbas Cluniacensis, qui proprii fratris interfectori non modo pepercit, sed etiam ad mortem quaesitum in mona- sterio suscepit, et sanctae conversionis habitum in- duit.
passages.english: Not to return evil for evil.] Because, as Origen, cited by Hildemar, says: "Worse is he who pays back in kind than he who does the evil in the first place." This instrument was perfectly fulfilled by St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, who not only spared the murderer of his own brother, but even, when the man was being sought for death, received him into the monastery and clothed him in the habit of holy conversion.

passages.original: Bernardus detractores comparat vulpibus, quae demoliuntur vi- neas; et Petrus Damiani locustis, 136 quae alienas fruges corrodunt, cum detractio aliud nihil sit quam respectu adetius gloriae minuendae mordax in atium delatio; unde et Cassianus perniciosam fratrum devo- rationem eam vocat. Quantum vero sit illa vitium ac peccatum, nec melius nec eloquentius aperire pos- sumus quam S. Bernardi verbis (Serm. 63. in Cant.): « Nunquid non vipera est lingua ista? ferocissima plane, nimirum quae tam lethaliter tres inficiat uno flatu.
passages.english: Bernard compares detractors to foxes that destroy the vineyards, and Peter Damian to locusts that gnaw away others' crops, since detraction is nothing other than a biting accusation against another with a view to diminishing his glory; hence Cassian too calls it a pernicious devouring of the brethren. How great a vice and sin it is, we cannot show better or more eloquently than in the words of St Bernard (Sermon 63 on the Song of Songs): "Is not that tongue a viper? Most ferocious indeed, since it so lethally poisons three with one breath.
passages.notes: 'respectu adetius gloriae minuendae mordax in atium delatio' is garbled; read as 'respectu alterius gloriae minuendae mordax in alium delatio'. '136' is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Denique quod proprium est hujus instrumenti, ad bene orandum, oratio debet esse frequens et assidua, ut multis nos Scriptura locis edocet: et certe « per- parum orat, quisquis illo tantum tempore, quo ge- nua flectuntur, orare consuevit, » inquit abbas Isaac apud Cassianum (Collat. 10, cap. 14).
passages.english: Finally, as regards what is proper to this instrument, for praying well prayer ought to be frequent and constant, as Scripture teaches us in many places; and certainly "he prays very little who is accustomed to pray only at the time when the knees are bent," says abbot Isaac in Cassian (Conference 10, ch. 14).

passages.original: 11 de divers.) : « Caveamus a propria voluntate tanquam a vipera pessima et nequissima, quae sola deinceps damnare possit animas nostras; » et alibi (Serm. 2 Temp. Pasch.): Cesset propria voluntas, et infernus non erit. » Et apud Cassianum (Coll. 24, c. 23) abbas Abraham : « Perditio nostra est oblectatio vitae praesentis, et, ut expressius dicam, exsecutio deside- riorum voluntatumque nostrarum. »
passages.english: 11 On Various Topics): "Let us beware of self-will as of a most evil and wicked viper, which alone can henceforth damn our souls"; and elsewhere (Sermon 2 for Eastertide): "Let self-will cease, and there will be no hell." And in Cassian (Conference 24, ch. 23) abbot Abraham [says]: "Our perdition is the delight of the present life and, to put it more plainly, the carrying out of our desires and wishes."
passages.notes: Opening '11' completes a citation begun in the preceding context (St Bernard, Sermon 11).

passages.original: Primo ergo, qui incorruptam servare castitatem desiderat, jejunio ante omnia corpus affligere debet, vulgare est enim proverbium : Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus; et econtra. Hino S. Ambrosius (Lib. i de Poen.) : « Libido, inquit, gravis ignis est, et ideo non debemus illi alimenta praebere. Luxuriae pasci- tur libido conviviis, nutritur deliciis, vino accendi- tur, ebrietate flammatur. » Et S. Joannes Climac. (Grad, 14) : « Qui servit ventri suo, et interim cona- tur spiritum luxuriae vincere, perinde facit atque is qui incendium vult oleo superare.
passages.english: First, then, whoever desires to keep chastity unimpaired must above all afflict the body with fasting, for it is a common proverb: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold; and conversely. Hence St Ambrose (Book I On Penance): "Lust," he says, "is a grievous fire, and therefore we must not give it fuel. Lust is fed by banquets of luxury, nourished by delicacies, kindled by wine, inflamed by drunkenness." And St John Climacus (Step 14): "He who serves his belly and meanwhile tries to overcome the spirit of lust acts just like one who wants to put out a fire with oil.
passages.notes: 'Hino' read as 'Hinc'.

passages.original: Unde, fratres eharissimi, ab omnibus Chris- tianis, praeeipue tamen clericis, sive monachis In- digna et inhonesta familiaritas fugienda est, quia sine ulla dubitatione qui familiaritatem non vult vitare suspectam, cito dilabitur in ruinam.» Et paulo post : « Quod autem libidinem fugiendam esse suggerimus, apostolus Paulus evidenter ostendit, qui cum omnibus vitiis praedicaverit resistendum, dum contra libidinem loqueretur, non dixit resistite, sed fugite fornicationem, ac sic contra reliqua vitia, Deo auxiliante, debemus in praesenti resistere, libidinem vero fugiendo superare, licet alibi in Scripturis di- vinis legimus : Noli, inquit, in faciem virginis inten- dere. ne te scandalizet vultus ejus. » Idem docent S. Hieronymus scribens adversus Vigilantium sub finem, et Cassianus lib. vi Institutionum, cap. 3; quibus concinit illud Goffridi abbatis Vindocinensis (Lib. iv, ep. 41) : «Ubi inordinate saecularis est assi- duitas, diu de ssc non creditur grandis intuitas. maxime in loco in quo sexus femineus habitare per- mittitur, per quem etiam religiosae personae suspectae nabentur.
passages.english: Therefore, dearest brothers, unworthy and indecent familiarity must be shunned by all Christians, but especially by clerics or monks, because beyond any doubt whoever will not avoid suspect familiarity quickly slips into ruin." And a little later: "That lust must be fled, as we urge, the apostle Paul plainly shows: though he preached that all vices must be resisted, when he spoke against lust he did not say 'resist' but 'flee fornication'. So against the other vices, with God's help, we ought to stand and resist in the present, but lust we must overcome by fleeing, as we also read elsewhere in the divine Scriptures: 'Do not,' it says, 'gaze on the face of a virgin, lest her countenance cause you to stumble.'" The same is taught by St Jerome writing against Vigilantius near the end, and by Cassian, Institutes Book VI, ch. 3; with whom agrees this from Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme (Book IV, letter 41): "Where there is disorderly constant association with the world, great integrity is not long believed to exist, especially in a place where the female sex is permitted to dwell, on account of which even religious persons are held suspect.
passages.notes: 'diu de ssc non creditur grandis intuitas' is corrupt; read as 'diu esse non creditur grandis integritas'. 'licet' rendered loosely as 'as also'.

passages.original: » Et S. Carilefus ad missos ab Ultrogotha regina ejus conspectu frui de- siderante : « Certum habeat, quandiu in corpore fuero, faciem me mulieris nequaquam visurum (In ejus Vita n. 28, saec. i). » Et apud Cassianum (Lib. ii, c. 17) : « Haec est antiquitus Patrum permanens nunc usque sententia.... Omnimodis monachum fu- gere debere mulieres, et episcopos, etc. » Episcopos quidem propter manuum impositionem; feminas propter periculum. Sed quia nonnunquam aliud sua- det necessitas, tunc quidem non nisi breviter, idque raro cum eis loqui permittit S.
passages.english: " And St. Carilefus [said] to those sent by Queen Ultrogotha, who desired to enjoy the sight of him: "Let her be certain that, as long as I am in the body, I shall never see the face of a woman (In his Life, n. 28, century 1)." And in Cassian (Book 2, ch. 17): "This is the opinion of the Fathers from of old, enduring even until now.... That a monk ought by all means to flee women and bishops, etc." Bishops, indeed, on account of the laying on of hands; women on account of the danger. But because necessity sometimes urges otherwise, then St.
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-sentence: "S." begins "S. Basilius" (St. Basil) in the following context. That sentence reads: "St. Basil permits speaking with them only briefly, and that rarely." "Episcopos propter manuum impositionem" refers to the fear of being ordained against one's will. "saec. i" probably refers to the first Benedictine saeculum of the Acta Sanctorum O.S.B.

Carilefus ad missos ab Ultrogotha regina ejus conspectu frui de- siderante : « Certum habeat, quandiu in corpore fuero, faciem me mulieris nequaquam visurum (In ejus Vita n. 28, saec. i). » Et apud Cassianum (Lib. ii, c. 17) : « Haec est antiquitus Patrum permanens nunc usque sententia.... Omnimodis monachum fu- gere debere mulieres, et episcop(??)s, etc. » Episcopos quidem propter manuum impositionem; feminas propter periculum. Sed quia nonnunquam aliud sua- det necessitas, tunc quidem non nisi breviter, idque raro cum eis loqui permittit S.
