And in Cassian (Book 2, ch. 17): "This is the opinion of the Fathers from of old, enduring even until now.... That a monk ought by all means to flee women and bishops, etc." Bishops, indeed, on account of the laying on of hands; women on account of the danger. But because necessity sometimes urges otherwise, then St.
passages.notes: "episcop(??)s" is read as "episcopos" (bishops). The passage ends mid-sentence: "S." begins "S. Basilius" (St. Basil) in the following context. That sentence reads: "St. Basil permits speaking with them only briefly, and that rarely."

passages.original: Tacere et audire discipulo convenit.] Hinc Scriptu- ra : Audi, inquit, tacens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi bona gratia (Eccli. xxxii). Plane primus phi- losophiae nuncupator et creditor Pythagoras acce- dentes discipulos nihil ante docuit quam tacere; primaque apud eum meditatio futuro sapienti erat linguam omnem coercere : unde et quinquennii si- lentium discipulis imponebat; quod illi, ut profa- nam discerent philosophiam, muti cum gaudio per- solvebant.
passages.english: "It befits the disciple to be silent and to listen." Hence Scripture says: "Listen in silence, and for your reverence good grace will come to you" (Ecclus. 32). Indeed Pythagoras, the first to give philosophy its name and to entrust himself to it, taught the disciples who came to him nothing before [he taught them] to be silent. With him, the first exercise for the future wise man was to restrain the tongue entirely. Hence he also imposed a five-year silence on his disciples, which they, in order to learn profane philosophy, discharged mute and with joy.
passages.notes: "creditor" is odd here; it is perhaps a corruption of "conditor" (founder).

passages.original: siquidem fieri solet plerumque, ut qui sese in rebus hujusmodi occupant, ii rectam rationem deserant; quippe cum ex eo illud fiat, ut animus ad ridicula diffundatur, et in tacita secum cogitatione gravitatis severitatisque nervos omnes elida(??). » Sanctus Hieronymus ad Nepotianum scribens (Epist. 2) : « Omnes delicias, et lepores, et risu dignas urbanitates, et caeteras ineptias amato- rum, in comoedis erubescimus, in saeculi hominibus detestamur; quanto magis in monachis et in clericis, quorum et sacerdotium proposito, et propositum or- natur sacerdotio! » S. Nicetius abbas et postea epi- scopus (Apud Gregor. Turon. I. de Vit. Pat., c. 17) : « Cavenda est scurrilitas, dilectissimi, et omne ver- bum otiosum, ut sicut corpus omne purum exhibere debemus Deo, ita etiam et os non ad aliud 191 nisi ad laudem Dei.
passages.english: for it usually happens that those who occupy themselves in things of this kind abandon right reason, since from this it comes about that the mind is dissipated into laughable things, and in its silent reflection within itself crushes all the sinews of gravity and seriousness." St. Jerome, writing to Nepotian (Letter 2): "All delights and witticisms and pleasantries worthy of laughter, and the other follies of lovers, we blush at in comedies and detest in men of the world; how much more in monks and clerics, whose priesthood is adorned by their profession, and whose profession by their priesthood!" St. Nicetius, abbot and afterwards bishop (in Gregory of Tours, Lives of the Fathers, ch. 17): "Buffoonery must be guarded against, most beloved, and every idle word, so that, just as we ought to present the whole body pure to God, so also the mouth, [opening it] for nothing else but the praise of God.
passages.notes: "elida(??)" is read as "elidat" (crushes). "191" is the page number of the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: 2), « Dum haec, inquit, Evangelii verba considero, quid aliud quam quoddam nobis com- mercium propositum esse perpendo? quia nimirum et momentaneo risu perpetuus fletus eruitur, et tem- porali fietu perpetua laetitia comparatur. » Hac sen- tentia deterrebantur Pachomiani, apud quos, teste Rufino (Lib, iiide Vit. Patr. 35), impossibile erat ali- quem verbum otiosum loqui. Hac deterrebantur SS. Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, et alter Macarius, quorum in Regula lego (Cap. 15) : « Si quis ex fra- tribus sermonem in congregatione otiosum emiserit, ne reus sit concilii, praecipimus eum triduo a fratrum congregatione vel colloquio esse alienum, ut nullus cum eo jungatur.
passages.english: 2): "When I consider these words of the Gospel," he says, "what else do I judge but that a kind of exchange is set before us? For indeed perpetual weeping is brought forth by momentary laughter, and perpetual joy is purchased by temporal weeping." By this saying the Pachomians were deterred, among whom, as Rufinus testifies (Lives of the Fathers, Book 3, 35), it was impossible for anyone to speak an idle word. By it were deterred Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius and the other Macarius, in whose Rule I read (ch. 15): "If any of the brothers utters an idle word in the community, so that he may not be liable to the council, we command that he be kept apart from the community or conversation of the brothers for three days, so that no one associates with him.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-citation: the "2" completes the reference to Peter Damian, Book 5, Letter 2. "reus sit concilii" echoes Matthew 5:22, "liable to the council".

passages.original: Benedicti percurrat, ibique duodecim humilitatis gradus satis luculenter expositos inveniet. » Est autem humilitas virtus, qua quis verissima sui co- gnitione sibi ipsi vilescit, sive, ut citatus a Boherio S. Augustinus ait : « Virtus, per quam animus in nullo se efferens, nihilque boni sibi ascribens, exte- rius etiam dejecti praefert habitum. »
passages.english: Benedict, and there he will find the twelve degrees of humility set out quite clearly." Humility is the virtue by which someone, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes worthless in his own eyes; or, as St. Augustine, cited by Boherius, says: "The virtue by which the mind, exalting itself in nothing and ascribing nothing good to itself, also displays outwardly the bearing of one cast down."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, completing "the Rule of St. Benedict" from the preceding context.

passages.original: Benedicto est timor Dei : « Pri- mus, infit Smaragdus, ordine, quia primus est in cogitatione, in corde et voluntate. » Primus, quia initium sapientiae omnisque virtutis limor Domini, ut loquitur Propheta; primus denique, quia, ut dicit Cassianus (Lib. iv, cap. 39), « principium nostrae sa- lutis, ejusdemque custodia timor Domini est; per hunc enim et initium conversionis, et vitiorum pur- gatio, et virtutum custodia bis qui imbuuntur ad viam perfectionis, acquiritur; qui dum penetraverit homi- nis mentem, contemptum rerum omnium parit, obli- vionem parentum, mundique ipsius gignit horrorem.
passages.english: Benedict is the fear of God. "First in order," says Smaragdus, "because it is first in thought, in heart and in will." First, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and of all virtue, as the Prophet says; first, finally, because, as Cassian says (Book 4, ch. 39), "the beginning of our salvation, and its safeguard, is the fear of the Lord. For through it the beginning of conversion, the purging of vices and the safeguarding of virtues are acquired by those who are being trained in the way of perfection. When it has penetrated a man's mind, it produces contempt of all things and forgetfulness of parents, and begets horror of the world itself.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. Joined with the preceding context it reads: "the first degree... for our holy father Benedict is the fear of God." "limor" is read as "timor" (fear), and "bis" as "his" (those).

passages.original: Et quia cogitatio hominis confitebitur tibi.] Id est cognoscetur a te. Nam « quia cogitatio nota est Deo, inquit Hildemarus, ipsa notitia dicitur Deo confiteri. » Quam expositionem sequitur Bern. Cassinensis, et confirmat Guido Juvenalis, hunc regulae textum ita Gal(??)ice reddens : La pensée de Chomme se montrera à toi et te fera hommage, car elle ne peut fuir ta con- naissance. Aliter tamen Smaragdus : « Cogitatio ho- minis, ait, tunc Deo confitetur, quando peccata prae- terita humili satisfactione ab illo damnantur;
passages.english: "And because the thought of man will confess to you." That is, it will be known by you. For "because thought is known to God," says Hildemar, "that very knowledge is said to confess to God." Bernard of Monte Cassino follows this interpretation, and Guido Juvenalis confirms it, rendering this text of the Rule into French thus: "The thought of man will show itself to you and will do you homage, for it cannot flee your knowledge." Smaragdus, however, [takes it] otherwise: "The thought of man," he says, "confesses to God when past sins are condemned before him with humble satisfaction;
passages.notes: "Gal(??)ice" is read as "Gallice" (into French), and "Chomme" as "l'homme" (man). "ab illo damnantur" could also be taken as "are condemned by him".

passages.original: Ergo si oc(??)li Domini.] Oculi Domini Smaragdo « respectio est divina, qua semper respicit super bo- nos, ut cos ab insidiis inimici defendat, a peccatis custodiat, et bonis jugiter operibus persistere faciat; » vel juxta Cassianum (Lib. viii, cap. 4) in oculis Dei « immensitatem perspicaciae, qua universa perlustrat et perspicit, et qu d nihil eum ex his quae ex nobis geruntur, gerendave sunt, seu cogitantur, lateat, scire possumus. » Absit enim ut corporeum aliquid in Deo existimemus, ut quondam voluerunt anthro- pomo philae, quorum errorem refutat Theodoretus quae l. 20 in Genesim. De his agunt Sozomenus, lib. viii, cap.
passages.english: "Therefore if the eyes of the Lord." The eyes of the Lord are, for Smaragdus, "the divine regard, by which he always looks upon the good, to defend them from the snares of the enemy, guard them from sins, and make them persist continually in good works." Or, according to Cassian (Book 8, ch. 4), in the eyes of God "we can recognise the immensity of his perceptiveness, by which he surveys and sees through all things, and [we can know] that nothing of what is done or is to be done by us, or is thought, escapes him." For far be it from us to suppose anything bodily in God, as the anthropomorphites once wished; Theodoret refutes their error in Question 20 on Genesis. Sozomen deals with them, Book 8, ch.
passages.notes: "oc(??)li" is read as "oculi" (eyes), "cos" as "eos" (them), "qu d" as "quod" (that), and "anthropomo philae" as "anthropomorphitae" (anthropomorphites). "quae l. 20" is taken as "quaest. 20" (Question 20). The final reference continues in the following context (ch. 11).

passages.original: Et si ab angelis nobis deputatis quotidie die noctuque Domino factori nostro opera nostra nuntiantur.] Nun- tiant ergo coelestes illi spiritus opera nostra Deo, 209 unde et angeli, id est nuntii dicuntur, non quasi ne- sciat Ille, sed « ut officium suum et ministerium im- pleant, quia nuntii sunt, » inquit Haimo Halbersta- tensis. Vel, ut ait Origenes : « Offerunt sancti angeli Dei, non quasi nesciat is qui omnia novit antequam fiant, sed ut testes efficiantur sanctitatis atque pie- talis justorum. Iterum lanquam deflentes impietates et injustitias injustorum, atque etiam ipsius diaboli;
passages.english: "And if our works are reported daily, day and night, to the Lord our maker by the angels assigned to us." So those heavenly spirits report our works to God, which is why they are called angels, that is, messengers. [They do this] not as though He did not know, but "so that they may fulfil their office and ministry, because they are messengers," says Haimo of Halberstadt. Or, as Origen says: "The holy angels make offering to God, not as though he who knows all things before they happen did not know, but so that they may become witnesses of the holiness and piety of the righteous; and again, as it were, lamenting the impieties and injustices of the unjust, and even of the devil himself;
passages.notes: "209" is the page number of the printed edition and has been omitted. "lanquam" is read as "tanquam" (as it were). "Offerunt" has no object expressed; it is perhaps "they offer [our works]."

passages.original: Sed vocem illam Domini factis imitetur dicentis : Non veni facere voluntatem meam, sed ejus qui misit me.] « Idcirco enim, ut ait apud Cassianum (Coll. 24, c. ulti- mo) abbas Abraham, Dominus noster ac Salvator, ut nobis amputandarum voluntatum nostrarum formam traderet. Non veni, inquit, facere voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me; et iterum : Non sicut ego volo, sed sicut in : quam virtutem illi spe- cialiter exercent, qui in coenobiis commorantes se- nioris reguntur imperio, qui nihil omnino arbitrio suo agunt, sed voluntas corum ex voluntate pendet abbatis.
passages.english: But let him imitate in deeds that saying of the Lord: I came not to do my own will, but [the will] of him who sent me.] "For this reason," as Abbot Abraham says in Cassian (Conf. 24, last chapter), "our Lord and Saviour, in order to hand on to us the pattern of cutting off our own wills, said: I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me; and again: Not as I will, but as you [will]. This virtue those especially practise who, dwelling in monasteries, are governed by the command of an elder, who do nothing at all by their own choice, but their will hangs on the will of the abbot.
passages.notes: "sed sicut in" appears corrupt; read as "sed sicut tu" ("but as you [will]"). "corum" read as "eorum".

passages.original: Sed et praeceptum Domini in adversis et injuriis per patientiam adimplentes, qui percussi in maxillam, praebent et aliam.] Ubi Smaragdus : « Qui in injuriis irrogatis non reddit malum pro malo, ille maxillam percutienti unam praebet et aliam. Apud Cassianum (Collat. 16, cap. 22) abbas Joseph per aliam intelli- git, non sinistram maxillam. sed aliam dextram moxil- lam, interiorem scilicet; ita « ut si exterior dextra tua impetum ferientis exceperit, interior quoque homo per humilitatis assensum dextram suam praebeat verberandam, compatiens exterioris hominis pas- sioni, et quodammodo succumbens atque subjiciens suum corpus ferientis injuriae, ne exterioris hominis caede, vel tacitus intra moveatur interior.
passages.english: But also fulfilling the Lord's command through patience in adversities and injuries, those who, struck on the cheek, offer the other too.] On which Smaragdus [says]: "He who does not return evil for evil when injuries are inflicted offers to the one who strikes him on one cheek the other also." In Cassian (Conf. 16, ch. 22) Abbot Joseph understands by "the other" not the left cheek but another right cheek, namely the inner one; so that "if your outer right [cheek] has received the blow of the striker, the inner man too, by the consent of humility, should offer his right [cheek] to be struck, suffering with the passion of the outer man, and in a way yielding and submitting his own body to the injury of the striker, so that the inner man may not be moved within, even silently, by the beating of the outer man.

passages.original: Quintus humilitatis gradus est, si omnes cogitatio- nes malas cordi suo advenientes, vel mala a se abs- conse commissa per humilem confessionem abbati non celaverit suo.] Unde et apud Cassianum 219 (Coll, 2, c. 10) abbas Moyses : « Humilitatis, inquit, haec erit prima probatio, si unicuique non solum quae agenda sunt, sed etiam quae cogitantur seniorum reserventur examini. » Et quidem recte omnino postquam in quarto humilitatis gradu patientiam in duris, contrariis, et irrogatis injuriis reposuit S. P. Benedictus, in quinto humilem constituit confessio- nem; quia difficile est ut qui patitur injuriam, aliquo indignationis aut murmurationis m(??) adversus inferentem non feratur, ad quem superandum non parum confert humilis confessio.
passages.english: The fifth degree of humility is if he does not conceal from his abbot, by humble confession, all the evil thoughts that come into his heart, or the evils he has committed in secret.] Hence also in Cassian (Conf. 2, ch. 10) Abbot Moses says: "This will be the first proof of humility, if not only what is to be done but also what is thought is laid open to the examination of the elders." And indeed quite rightly, after our holy Father Benedict placed patience in hard and adverse things and in injuries inflicted in the fourth degree of humility, he set humble confession in the fifth; because it is difficult for one who suffers injury not to be carried by some movement of indignation or murmuring against the one who inflicts it, and for overcoming this humble confession helps not a little.
passages.notes: "m(??)" is illegible; probably "motu" ("movement").

passages.original: Benedictus instituit de humili ad abbatem conscientiae manifestatione, eadem prae- scripta offendes in Regula S. Antonii, n. 25, in ejus Vita, cap. 29; in Regula abbatis Isaiae, cap. 6; in Regulis fusius disputatis S. Basilli, cap. 26; apud Cassianum, lib. iv Institut., cap. 9, et collat. 2, cap. 10; apud S. passages.notes: Sentence begins mid-clause ("[What] St Benedict established here...") and ends mid-name, continued in the following context (Fructuosus).

passages.original: Ita nimirum S. Basilius : « Humilitas est, in- quit, omnes seipso 228 superiores existimare. » Et alibi (Reg. brev., inter. 198) : « Humilis omnes ter- renos honores respuens ultimum se judicat. » S. Ambrosius : « Haec est enim humilitas, si nihil sibi quis arroget; sed inferiorem se esse existimet. » S. Joannes Chysostomus (Homil. 33, super Genes.) : « Non eis tantum, qui aetate nobis sunt majores vel etiam aequales, honorem exhibeamus : non enim est humilitas quod facere debes necessitate;
passages.english: Thus indeed St Basil says: "Humility is to consider all [people] superior to oneself." And elsewhere (Shorter Rules, question 198): "The humble man, rejecting all earthly honours, judges himself the last." St Ambrose: "For this is humility, if one claims nothing for oneself but considers oneself to be inferior." St John Chrysostom (Homily 33 on Genesis): "Let us show honour not only to those who are older than us or even equal; for it is not humility [to do] what you must do out of necessity;
passages.notes: "Chysostomus" read as Chrysostomus.

Dei, quae in 229 aliis latent : unde Augustinus dicit in lib. de Virginitate : Existimate alios in oc- culto superior(??)s, quibus estis in manifesto n eliores. » Et certe ut hic citatus dicit alibi S. Augustinus (Lib. 85, quaest. 71) : « Illud cogitandum nullum esse ho- minem, qui non possit habere aliquod bonum, etiamsi lateat, in quo possit esse superior;
passages.english: 161, a. 6, ad 1): "Someone can without falsehood believe and declare himself more vile than all, according to the hidden defects which he knows in himself and the gifts of God which lie hidden in others: hence Augustine says in the book On Virginity: Consider others superior in secret, to whom you are better openly." And certainly, as St Augustine, cited here, says elsewhere (Book of 83 Questions, q. 71): "It must be reflected that there is no man who cannot have some good, even if it lies hidden, in which he may be superior;
passages.notes: Illegible letters restored: "viliorem", "dona", "superiores", "meliores". The text reads "Lib. 85, quaest."; Augustine's work is the 83 Questions, so 85 is probably a misprint.

passages.original: quia multos videas qui se omnium peccatores maximos praedicant, ad infernum usque deprimunt; quos si vel minimo tetig ris verbo, excandescentes injuriam sibi f(??)eri conqueruntur; quos non tam humiles, quam humilitatis larvas dixeris. Talis erat monachus ille apud Cassianum (Collat. 18, cap. 11), qui cum se plu(??)imum verbis depressisset, ita ut nec communem spirare aerem dignum se clamaret; admonitus a Serapione ne vagaretur oti(??)sus, sed in cella consi- steret, ferre haud potuit, nec dissimulare dolorem.
passages.english: for you may see many who proclaim themselves the greatest sinners of all and press themselves down to hell itself; yet if you touch them with even the slightest word, they flare up and complain that injury is being done them; you would call them not so much humble as masks of humility. Such was that monk in Cassian (Conf. 18, ch. 11) who, after he had greatly abased himself in words, so that he cried out he was not worthy even to breathe the common air, when admonished by Serapion not to wander about idle but to stay in his cell, could not bear it, nor hide his resentment.

passages.original: Talem et ipsi daemones habere possunt humilitatem, quam ipsa nostri cognitio exigit, et habere nos cogit veritas, humilitatem scilicet oris et intel ectus, non humilitatem cordis; humilitatem veritatis, non humi- litatem amoris. Quid igitur? « Vera est humilitas cordis retinendi, inquit apud Cassianum (Collat. 18, c. 11) abbas Piammon, quae non de affectata co poris atque verborum, sed ex int ma mentis humiliatione descendit, quae tunc demum evidentissimis patientiae 232 suae fulgebi indiciis, cum quis non ipse de se cri- mina ab aliis non credenda jactaverit, sed ab aliis ar- roganter ingesta et irrogatas injurias mansueta cordis aequanimitate toleraverit. » Talem a Caelant(??)a S. Hie- ronymus requirebat, cum diceret (Epist.
passages.english: Even the demons themselves can have such humility as knowledge of ourselves demands and truth compels us to have, namely humility of mouth and of intellect, not humility of heart; humility of truth, not humility of love. What then? "True humility of heart must be held fast," says Abbot Piammon in Cassian (Conf. 18, ch. 11), "which comes down not from an affected [humility] of body and words but from the inmost humbling of the mind; which will shine forth by the clearest signs of its patience only when someone does not boast of crimes about himself which others would not believe, but bears with gentle evenness of heart the insults arrogantly heaped on him by others and the injuries inflicted." Such [humility] St Jerome required of Celantia, when he said (Letter
passages.notes: "retinendi" read as "retinenda".

passages.original: et ex Bernardo Cassinensi commune monasterium est coenobium, in quo vivitur in com- muni a multis. Et sic hoc sensu octavo humilitatis gradu 233 praecipitur, ut monachus sive coenobita suo contentus statu, temere non appetat anachore- tarum vivendi rationem : « Superbus enim, ut ait Cassianus (Lib. xii, c. 30), « ipsam disciplinam coe- nobii perhorrescit, ac veluti fratrum consortio de perfectione retrahatur, ae de bono patientiae atque humilitatis aliorum vitio et impedimento revocetur, habitationem solitariae cellae desiderat, » quam supra vires sua pro(??)piciens humilis, in aliis quidem vene- ratur, sed pro se appetere non praesumit.
passages.english: and according to Bernard of Cassino, the common monastery is the cenobium, in which many live in common. And thus in this sense it is prescribed in the eighth degree of humility that the monk or cenobite, content with his own state, should not rashly seek the anchorites' way of living: "For the proud man," as Cassian says (Book 12, ch. 30), "shudders at the very discipline of the cenobium, and as if he were drawn back from perfection by the company of the brethren, and called away from the good of patience and humility by the fault and hindrance of others, he longs for the dwelling of a solitary cell," which the humble man, seeing it to be beyond his strength, reveres indeed in others but does not presume to seek for himself.
passages.notes: "ae" read as "ac"; "pro(??)piciens" as "prospiciens".

passages.original: Secunda ratio est, quia quidquid contra communis mona terii regulam praesumitur, a maligno spiritu esse dignoscitur, ut docet inter alios Cassianus (Collat. 18, cap. 3), eleganterque describit S. Ber- nardus his verbis (Serm. 33, in Cant.) : « Quoties, verbi gratia, suggessit anticipare vigilias, quo ad so- lemnia fratrum illuderet dormitanti?
passages.english: The second reason is that whatever is presumed against the rule of the common monastery is recognised to be from the evil spirit, as Cassian among others teaches (Conf. 18, ch. 3), and St Bernard describes elegantly in these words (Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs): "How often, for example, has he suggested anticipating the vigils, so as to mock [the monk] dozing at the solemn [offices] of the brethren?

passages.original: Ergo hii omnibus humilitatis gradibus ascensis, mo- nachus mox ad charitatem Dei perveniet illam.] Ergo via ad charitatem humilitas. Via utique vera ei sola; unde S. Augustinus : « Cogitas magnam fabricam construere celsitudinis? de fundamento prius cogita humilitatis,... hoc in te fode fundamentum humili· talis, et pervenies ad fastigium charitalis. » S. Ber- nardus (Epist. 42): « Ut castitas seu charitas detur, humilitas meretur, elc. » Et quidam ex antiquis Patribus (Ruffin.
passages.english: ["Therefore, when all these steps of humility have been climbed, the monk will soon arrive at that love of God."] Therefore humility is the way to charity. It is indeed the true and only way to it; hence St Augustine: "Are you thinking of building a great structure of height? First think of the foundation of humility... dig this foundation of humility in yourself, and you will reach the summit of charity." St Bernard (Letter 42): "Humility merits that chastity or charity be given, etc." And one of the ancient Fathers (Rufinus,
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (hii for hic, ei for et, charitalis, elc.). The passage ends mid-citation; the reference continues in the following text.

passages.original: An vero ita intellexerit Nico- laus de Fractura, cum facta sibi objectione, « quod si non indigeat psalmis vel lectione intendere, nun- quid in lectis ad pausandum se ponent? » respondet : « Dicas quod non, quia etsi non indigeant psalmis, vel lectionibus, seu orationibus quoad doctrinam eorum, indigent tamen ipsis 252 quoad salutem animarum ipsorum; et propterea dicit Hieronymus ad Rusticum monachum : Nunquam de manu tua cadat psalterium. » Caeterum hic praeterire non possum quod de piis Sanctigallensis monasterii Notkero, Rat- perto et Tutilone monachis scribit Ekkehardus ju- nior (In Vita Notkeri, n.
passages.english: But whether Nicholas de Fractura understood it in this way [may be asked], since, when the objection was put to him, "if they do not need to apply themselves to psalms or reading, will they then lie down on their beds to rest?", he replies: "Say no, because even if they do not need psalms, or readings, or prayers as regards their instruction, they nevertheless need them as regards the salvation of their souls; and therefore Jerome says to Rusticus the monk: Let the psalter never fall from your hand." Besides, I cannot pass over here what Ekkehard the Younger writes about the devout monks of the monastery of St Gall, Notker, Ratpert and Tutilo (in the Life of Notker, n.
passages.notes: "252" is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted. The sentence beginning "An vero" is elliptical; "[may be asked]" supplied. "Nicholas de Fractura" is given as in the text, unidentified further.

passages.original: Ex dictis hactenus constat perfectum S. Benedicti discipulum post nocturnas vigilias lectum non posse repetere; id quod tum antiquis tum recentioribus mo- nachis sub magna districtione cautum videmus : nam S. Chrysostomus monachorum sui temporis vitam de- scribens (Homil. 59, ad popul. Antioch.), « cum matuti- nas orationes et hymnos celebraverint, inquit, ad Scripturarum lectionem convertuntur. » Idem de Aegyp- tiis monachis asserit Cassianus in lib. ii, cap. 12. Re- fert etiam Ruffinus (Lib. iiide Vit. Ρat., n. 199) non- nullos fratres, quatuor nocte horis somno, quatuor psalmis, quatuor labori manuum operam dedisse, S. Caesarius in Regula ad virgines, qualis est apud Bol- landum Jan.
passages.english: From what has been said so far it is clear that a perfect disciple of St. Benedict cannot return to bed after the night vigils; and this, we see, was provided for under strict discipline both by ancient and by more recent monks. For St. Chrysostom, describing the life of the monks of his time (Homily 59, to the people of Antioch), says: "When they have celebrated the morning prayers and hymns, they turn to the reading of the Scriptures." Cassian asserts the same of the Egyptian monks in book 2, chapter 12. Rufinus also reports (Book 3 of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 199) that some brothers gave four hours of the night to sleep, four to psalms, and four to the work of their hands. St. Caesarius, in the Rule for virgins, as it appears in Bollandus, January
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-reference ("Jan."); the date (12) continues in the following context. "Homil. 59" and "iiide" are read as Homily 59 and "iii de" (book 3 of).

passages.original: Istud autem institutum antiquis monachis, ut vi- dimus hactenus, inviolabile 254 duplici ex causa commendat Joannes Cassianus : 1° ne purificationem nostram nocturnis orationibus acquisitam invidus hostis illusione somni contaminet; 2° ne somnus ille inertiam in monacho parturiat, ac per totum diem vigorem ejus obtundat, cordis pinguedinem exhau- riat, et debilem reddat eum adversus insidias inimici.
passages.english: This practice, which, as we have seen so far, was inviolable for the ancient monks, John Cassian commends for a twofold reason: first, so that the envious enemy may not defile through an illusion of sleep the purification we have acquired by the night prayers; second, so that that sleep may not give birth to sluggishness in the monk, and dull his vigour through the whole day, drain the richness of his heart, and make him weak against the snares of the enemy.
passages.notes: Page number "254" omitted. "cordis pinguedinem exhauriat" could also mean "drain off" in a positive sense; rendered literally.

passages.original: De dominicis diebus major videtur difficultas. Ut quid enim (??)aturius surgere, et matutinas laudes cum vigiliis uno tenore decurrere, nisi ut postea fes- sis corporibus aliqua concedatur requies? Adde quod veteres monachi, teste Cassiano, quos in multis S. Benedictus aemulatus est, sabbato post nocturnas vigilias duabus circiter horis dormirent; et ex Regu- la Pauli et Stephani (Lib, i, cap, 8), « mane dicta prima nullus se in lecto recubitet, excepto die domi- nico aut festis diebus, in quibus vigiliarum labore, et praeteriti di(??)i solito amplius fatigati paululum post primam qui ex vobis voluerint membra ponant in lectulis, quod non omni tempore idipsum, sed tantum aestivis mensibus liceat.
passages.english: Concerning Sundays the difficulty seems greater. For why rise earlier and run through Lauds together with the vigils in one continuous course, unless so that afterwards some rest may be granted to tired bodies? Add that the old monks, on the testimony of Cassian, whom St Benedict imitated in many things, slept for about two hours on Saturday after the night vigils; and from the Rule of Paul and Stephen (Book 1, ch. 8): "In the morning, when Prime has been said, let no one lie down in bed, except on Sunday or on feast days, on which, being more tired than usual from the labour of the vigils and of the previous day, those of you who wish may lay their limbs on their beds for a little while after Prime; but this is not to be permitted at every season, only in the summer months.
passages.notes: "(??)aturius" read as maturius (earlier); "di(??)i" read as diei. The quotation closes in the following text.

Ar- senius (Tom.

passages.notes: "an iquum" read as antiquum; "postiemas" as postremas; "reliciebant" as reficiebant. The reference continues in the following text.

passages.original: Aliquando duo sub una Gloria dicebantur psalmi, ut praescribit Regula S. Benedicti, sed id fieri prohi- bet Regula Magistri cap. 33. In Oriente hac Trinitatis glorificatione antiphonas tantummodo terminare so- lebant, ut scribit Cassianus. Denique in fine ultimi responsorii cujuscunque nocturni a S. Benedicto de- cernitur dici, atque in responsoriis crebrius a Roma- nis usurpari asserit Walfridus cap. 25. De hoc versi culo tractatum Anagogicum edidit Joannes Gerson, quem consule, si(??)lubet, tom.
passages.english: Sometimes two psalms were said under one Gloria, as the Rule of St Benedict prescribes, but the Rule of the Master forbids this to be done, ch. 33. In the East they used to end only antiphons with this glorification of the Trinity, as Cassian writes. Finally, St Benedict decrees that it be said at the end of the last responsory of every nocturn, and Walafrid, ch. 25, asserts that it was used rather frequently by the Romans in responsories. On this verse John Gerson published an anagogical treatise, which you may consult, if you like, vol.
passages.notes: The reference continues in the following text (vol. III, On the Hymn of Glory).

passages.original: Post hunc psalmus nonagesimus quartus.] Invitato- rius appellari solitus, quem Regula Magistri Respon- sorium hortationis, S. Isidorus in officio Mozarabo Sonum vocat. Hunc in ipso divini officii exordio ante S. Benedicti tempora recitatum fuisse constat ex S. Athanasio testante (Serm. de Deipara) Christianos ad precum principium invitantes invicem et adhortantes, clamare solitos verba hujus psalmi.
passages.english: ["After this, the ninety-fourth psalm."] Usually called the Invitatory, which the Rule of the Master calls the Responsory of Exhortation, and St Isidore, in the Mozarabic office, calls the Sonus. That it was recited at the very beginning of the divine office before the time of St Benedict is clear from St Athanasius, who testifies (Sermon on the Mother of God) that Christians, inviting and exhorting one another at the start of prayers, used to cry out the words of this psalm.

Ambrosio compositi ejus tempore frequentius cantari coeperunt, ut ipse testatur in fine concionis de Ba- silicis non tradendis haereticis. The last explanation is illustrated by Amalarius in the aforesaid Supplement, writing thus: "It is shown with a certain certainty, in a way, that St

passages.english: 14, on 1 Timothy): "When the cock gives its cry before daylight, all, shaking off sleep, rise with reverence, roused by their superior; and they stand in the sacred choir, and at once with outstretched hands they sing the holy hymns together"; in Cassian, who relates (Book 2, ch. 12) that the one who chanted the psalms, while the others listened and sat, sang them standing; in the Rule of the Master (ch. 47): "The one chanting the psalms should stand with body motionless and head bowed, and sing praises to the Lord with moderation;
passages.notes: Begins mid-citation of Chrysostom's homily; quotation closes in the following text.

passages.original: quia fuerunt multi nominati, et ta- men in eorum libris inventus est error; et ideo dixit a nominatissimis, ac si diceret, illorum doctorum legant expositiones quorum in libris non invenitur error, sicut est Augustinus, et Gregorius, sive Am- brosius, et caeteri alii Patres catholici. » Nicolao de Fractura doctores nominatissimi sunt Gregorius, Augustinus, Hieronymus, Ambrosius. Addit tamen : « Alii enim doctores, ut est Hilarius, Basilius, Joannes Chrysost., Gregorius Nazianzenus, Beda presbyter, nominatissimi similiter possunt dici, ex eo quod eorum dicta sunt ab Ecclesia approbata, etc. »
passages.english: because there were many who were renowned, and yet error has been found in their books; and therefore he said 'by the most renowned', as if to say: let them read the expositions of those doctors in whose books no error is found, such as Augustine, and Gregory, or Ambrose, and the other catholic Fathers." For Nicholas de Fractura the most renowned doctors are Gregory, Augustine, Jerome and Ambrose. He adds, however: "For other doctors, such as Hilary, Basil, John Chrysostom, Gregory Nazianzen and Bede the priest, can likewise be called most renowned, from the fact that their sayings have been approved by the Church, etc."
passages.notes: Continues Hildemar's quotation from the context.

passages.original: 3 Mart.), Hanc- que olim fuisse communem monasteriorum consue- tudinem discimus ex Amalarii Supplemento, in quo haec habet : « Omnibus enim dominicis Resurrectio- nis diebus recte a monachis circa mediam noctem surgitur. » Et prius dixerat S. P. Benedictum id ac- cepisse a S. Ambrosio, « cui, inquit, semper con- suetudo fuit dominicis diebus ante horam noctis me- diam surgere : quod hymnus ejus demonstrat : Sur- gamus omnes ocius, Et nocte quaeramus pium. » In Cisterciensi vero anni 1429 capitulo generali statu- tum est ut dominicis festisque diebus una hora citius solito surgatur.
passages.english: 3 March). And we learn that this was once the common custom of monasteries from the Supplement of Amalarius, in which he has the following: "For on all Sundays, the days of the Resurrection, monks rightly rise around midnight." And earlier he had said that the holy father Benedict took this from St Ambrose, "whose custom," he says, "was always to rise on Sundays before the middle hour of the night, as his hymn shows: 'Let us all rise more swiftly, and seek the Holy One by night.'" But in the Cistercian general chapter of the year 1429 it was decreed that on Sundays and feast days they should rise one hour earlier than usual.
passages.notes: The opening '3 Mart.)' closes a citation (Bollandists, 3 March) begun in the preceding context.

passages.original: Verum cum illud Chronicon stylo Dacii tempora non redoleat, et alio- quin falsa plurima contineat, illius foetus non esse apud eruditos quosque pro certo habetur, ac proinde quae de composito ab Ambrosio et Augustino hymno Te Deum laudamus narrantur, dubiae omnino, ne di- cam nullius, sunt fidei. Quis autem illius sit auctor hactenus incompertum est. Solus a Smaragdo et aliis quibusdam creditur Ambrosius. Sed in Abbonis ab- batis Floriacensis epistola nondum edita tribuitur S. Hilario, ut docuit me, qui ex nostris novae operum hujus sancti editioni adornandae laborat.
passages.english: But since that Chronicle does not have the flavour of the style of Dacius's times, and besides contains a great many falsehoods, it is held for certain among all the learned not to be his offspring; and therefore what is related about the hymn Te Deum laudamus being composed by Ambrose and Augustine is of entirely doubtful credibility, not to say of none. Who its author is, however, has so far not been discovered. Smaragdus and certain others believe it to be Ambrose alone. But in a still unpublished letter of Abbo, abbot of Fleury, it is attributed to St Hilary, as I was informed by one of our [brethren] who is labouring to prepare the new edition of this saint's works.

passages.original: Sed inveni tandem qui nodum solveret Amalarium Fortunatum : Episcopus, Inquit (Lib.ii, cap. 9), vel sacerdos dicit, Oremus, ac deinde subsequitur benedictio. Utroque nomine benedictionis et orationis vocatur oratio sacerdotis. De benedictione dicit Apostolus : Si benedixeris spi- ritu, qui supplet locum idiotae quomodo dicit amen super tuam benedictionem, quia284nescit quid di- cas? Hanc benedictionem vocat Ambrosius oratio- nem, dicens : « Imperitus audiens quod non intelli- git, nescit finem orationis, et non respondet amen, id est verum, ut confirmetur benedictio. » Idem paulo post confirmat auctoritate S. Augustini, benedictio- nem pro oratione usurpantis (De Dono persever., c. 23) : « An quis sacerdotem super fideles Dominum invocantem, si quando dixit, Da illi, Domine, in te perseverare usque in finem, non solum voce ausus est, sed saltem cogitatione reprehendere, ac non potius super talem ejus benedictionem et corde credente, et ore confitente respondit, amen.
passages.english: But at last I found someone to untie the knot, Amalarius Fortunatus. "The bishop," he says (Book II, ch. 9), "or the priest says 'Let us pray', and then the blessing follows. The priest's prayer is called by both names, blessing and prayer. Of the blessing the Apostle says: 'If you bless with the spirit, how does he who fills the place of the unlearned say amen over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?' This blessing Ambrose calls a prayer, saying: 'The unskilled man, hearing what he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer, and does not answer amen, that is, "true", so that the blessing may be confirmed.'" He confirms the same a little later by the authority of St Augustine, who uses 'blessing' for 'prayer' (On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 23): "Or has anyone dared to find fault, not only with his voice but even in thought, with a priest calling on the Lord over the faithful, if ever he said, 'Grant him, Lord, to persevere in you to the end', and has he not rather answered amen over such a blessing of his, both with believing heart and confessing mouth?
passages.notes: The closing quotation mark of Augustine's question falls in the following context.

passages.original: eosque in plurali laudes appellat, sive quia plures sunt psalmi, ut dicit in primo comment. Boherius; sive quia plu- ries ad laudes Creatoris invitamur. Hos psalmos mane recitabant AEgyptii monachi, testante Cassiano lib. iii, c. 6. Sed et S. Caesarius in Regula ad mo- nachos c. 2 praescribit ut ad matutinos dicant Bene- dictionem; Laudate Dominum de coelis.
passages.english: and he calls them in the plural 'lauds', either because there are several psalms, as Boherius says in his first commentary, or because we are invited several times to the praises of the Creator. The Egyptian monks recited these psalms in the morning, as Cassian testifies, Book III, ch. 6. And St Caesarius too, in his Rule for monks, ch. 2, prescribes that at matins they say the Benedicite [and] Laudate Dominum de coelis.
passages.notes: 'Benedictionem' here refers to the canticle Benedicite (Song of the Three Children).

passages.original: 64, in append.) seu quivis alius : « Haec oratio compendiosis verbis, id est septem petitionibus omnes species orationis comprehendit, quibus Deum interpellamus aut pro appetendis bonis, aut pro vi- tandis malis, aut pro delendis commissis. » Quae tria fuse et apte ex SS. Patribus explicat Alardus Gazaeus ad Cassiani collat. 9, c. 18. Et has forte ob praerogati- vas « mos apostolorum fuit, inquit S. Gregorius, ut ad ipsam solummodo orationem (dominicam) oblatio- nis hostiam consecrarent. » S. Clemens in Constit.
passages.english: 64, in the appendix) or whoever else [wrote it]: "This prayer, in concise words, that is, in seven petitions, embraces all kinds of prayer by which we entreat God, either for goods to be sought, or for evils to be avoided, or for sins committed to be blotted out." These three things Alardus Gazaeus explains at length and aptly from the holy Fathers on Cassian's Conference 9, ch. 18. And perhaps on account of these prerogatives "it was the custom of the apostles," says St Gregory, "to consecrate the victim of the offering at this prayer (the Lord's) alone." St Clement in the Constitutions
passages.notes: Begins and ends mid-citation (Augustine, Sermon 64 in the appendix; Apostolic Constitutions).

passages.original: 2) in primitiva Ecclesia post quamlibet horam absque alia oratione alia voce pronuntiatam fuisse, quod adhuc, inquit, Ecclesia Lateranensis dicitur obser- vare. Eamdem alta voce in ecclesia cantatam fuisse innuit abbas Isaac apud Cassianum (Collat. 9, cap. 22), cum exponens illa verba, Et dimitte nobis debita nostra, etc., sic loquitur : « Tantum remittitur nobis quantum nos remiserimus eis, qui nobis quacunque malignitate nocuerant; quod formidantes nonnulli cum in ecclesia haec oratio ab universa plebe conci- nitur, hunc locum taciti praetermittunt, ut semet- ipsos obligare potius quam excusare sua professione videantur.
passages.english: 2) that in the primitive Church after each hour it was pronounced aloud without any other prayer, which, he says, the Church of the Lateran is said still to observe. That the same was sung aloud in church is suggested by abbot Isaac in Cassian (Conference 9, ch. 22), when, expounding the words 'And forgive us our debts', etc., he speaks thus: "As much is forgiven us as we have forgiven those who had harmed us by any malice whatever; fearing this, some, when this prayer is sung together by the whole people in church, pass over this passage in silence, lest they should seem by their own declaration to bind themselves rather than excuse themselves.
passages.notes: 'alia voce' is evidently a misprint for 'alta voce' (aloud). Final clause in the Latin reads literally 'so that they may seem to bind rather than excuse'; 'ne' (lest) seems required, as in the next unit.

passages.original: Per ipsius orationis sponsionem, etc.] Id est pactum quod Deus nobiscum, et nos cum Deo quasi fecisse dicimur, ut ipse dimittat nobis si dimiserimus, non dimittat si non dimiserimus. Hic respexisse videtur S. Benedictus ad eos qui, ut dicebat modo abbas Isaac apud Cassianum, cum dominica oratio ab uni- versa plebe concineretur, locum hunc taciti praeter- mittebant, ne semetipsos obligare potius quam excu- sare sua professione videretur.
passages.english: Through the pledge of this very prayer, etc.] That is, the pact which God is said, as it were, to have made with us and we with God: that he will forgive us if we have forgiven, and will not forgive if we have not forgiven. Here St Benedict seems to have had in view those who, as abbot Isaac in Cassian was just saying, when the Lord's prayer was sung together by the whole people, passed over this passage in silence, lest they should seem by their own declaration to bind themselves rather than excuse themselves.

passages.original: Tabennenses monachi tres quotidie persolvebant horas canonicas, vigilias nocturnas, nonam, et ve- speras, ut docet Palladius in Lausiaca c. 38. Toti- dem sabbato et dominica celebrabant AEgyptii mona- chi, in quibus praeter nocturnas vigilias et vesperas, hora tertia sacrae communionis obtentu, ut scribit Cassianus (Lib.iii, cap. 2) conveniebant.
passages.english: The monks of Tabennesi performed three canonical hours daily, the night vigils, none, and vespers, as Palladius teaches in the Lausiac [History], ch. 38. The Egyptian monks celebrated the same number on Saturday and Sunday, on which, besides the night vigils and vespers, they assembled at the third hour for the sake of holy communion, as Cassian writes (Book III, ch. 2).

passages.original: Aurelianus ad Regulae calcem scripsit ordinem psalmodiae a suis monachis servandum, in quo se- ptem notat horas canonicas, mentionemque facit tertiae, sextae, nonae, lucernarii, duodecimae, noctur- norum et matutinorum. Eumdem numerum horarum, licet diversis temporibus persolvendarum, in suo mo- nasterio observatum fuisse docet Cassianus (Lib.iiicap. 3, 4 et 5); celebrabant enim nocturnas vigilias, matutinos, qui ad auroram dicebantur; alios matu- tinos, qui nostrae primae respondebant, quosque suo tempore institutos fuisse testatur, tertiam, sextam, nonam, et vesperas. Similem etiam numerum in monachis sui temporis agnovit Cassiodorus, cum scribens in psalmum cxviii, exponensque illum ver- siculum : Septies in die laudem dixi tibi, sic loqui- tur : « Si ad litteram hunc numerum velimus adver- tere, septem illas significat vices quibas se monacho- rum devotio consolatur, id est, matutinas, tertiam, sex- tam, nonam, lucernarium, completorios, nocturnos. » 303 Similes horas instituit Regula S. Isidori, cap. 7. Denique S.
passages.english: Aurelian, at the end of his Rule, wrote an order of psalmody to be kept by his monks, in which he notes seven canonical hours, and makes mention of terce, sext, none, the lucernarium, the twelfth [hour], nocturns and matins. Cassian teaches (Book III, ch. 3, 4 and 5) that the same number of hours, though to be performed at different times, was observed in his monastery; for they celebrated the night vigils; matins, which were said at dawn; another matins, corresponding to our prime, which he testifies had been instituted in his own time; terce, sext, none, and vespers. Cassiodorus too recognised a similar number among the monks of his time, when, writing on Psalm 118 and expounding the verse 'Seven times a day I have praised you', he speaks thus: "If we wish to take this number literally, it signifies those seven times with which the devotion of monks consoles itself, that is, matins, terce, sext, none, lucernarium, compline, nocturns." The Rule of St Isidore, ch. 7, established similar hours. Finally St
passages.notes: '303' is a page number of the printed edition, omitted. The sentence breaks off at 'S.' (continuing 'Basil' in the next context).

passages.original: Tertio, missa sumitur pro hora canonica, sive pro cursu divini officii. Sic apud Cassianum (Lib.ii, cap. 13) : « Quare post missam nocturnam dormire non oporteat. » Et alibi (Lib.iii, cap. 5) : « Missa canonica celebrata, usque ad lucem post haec vigi- lias extendunt. » Et concilium Agathense (Can. 30) : « Hymni matutini vel vespertini diebus omnibus de- cantentur, et in conclusione matutinarum vel ves- pertinarum missarum post hymnos capitella de psal- mis dicantur.
passages.english: Third, 'mass' (missa) is taken for a canonical hour, or for the course of the divine office. So in Cassian (Book II, ch. 13): "Why one ought not to sleep after the night missa." And elsewhere (Book III, ch. 5): "When the canonical missa has been celebrated, they extend the vigils after this until daylight." And the council of Agde (Canon 30): "Let the morning or evening hymns be sung on all days, and at the conclusion of the morning or evening missae, after the hymns, let short chapters from the psalms be said.
passages.notes: 'missa' here means an office or its dismissal, not the Eucharist.

passages.original: Sexto, denique, missa pro dimissione dicitur, sicut apud Tullium, v de Orat., collecta pro collectione; apud Tertull., I. iii cont. Marc., proba pro proba- tione; apud Cyprianum, remissa pro remissione.
passages.english: Sixth, finally, *missa* is said for *dimissio* (dismissal), just as in Tully (Cicero), book 5 of *On the Orator*, *collecta* [is used] for *collectio*; in Tertullian, book 3 *Against Marcion*, *proba* for *probatio*; in Cyprian, *remissa* for *remissio*.
passages.notes: Cicero's De Oratore has only three books; the reference 'v de Orat.' may be an error in the source.

passages.original: Joan- nes Craesbeeck : « Missae sint, hoc est orationes fiant, et mittantur ad Deum tum a singulis privatim, et submisse dicentibus Pater noster, etc; tum com- muniter uno sacerdote collectam clare recitante; di- cuntur enim orationes nostrae missae, » etc. Hugo Menardus : « Missae hoc loco collectae sunt seu ora- tiones, quae juxta Cassianum ad finem cujusque psal- mi dicebantur a sacerdote, quarum 310 mentionem tantum facit in fine horarum S. P. Benedictus brevi- tatis causa, tanquam rei suis monachis vulgaris et tritae, quemadmodum postea agit de brevi oratio(??) veluti obiter et per transennam, tanquam de re mo- nachis nota, quae majori explicatione non indigeat.
passages.english: Joannes Craesbeeck: "Let there be *missae*, that is, let prayers be made and sent to God, both by individuals privately, saying the Our Father etc. in a low voice, and in common, with one priest reciting the collect aloud; for our prayers are called *missae*," etc. Hugo Menardus: "*Missae* in this place are collects or prayers, which according to Cassian were said by the priest at the end of each psalm; our holy father Benedict merely mentions them at the end of the hours for the sake of brevity, as something common and familiar to his monks, just as afterwards he treats of short prayer as if in passing and cursorily, as of a thing known to monks, which needs no fuller explanation.
passages.notes: '310' is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted. 'oratio(??)' read as 'oratione'.

passages.original: Sed in puritate cordis.] Quia soli mundo corde Deum videbunt. « Ut autem eo fervore ac puritate qua de- bet, emitti possit oratio (ita loquitur Cassianus [Collat. 9, c. 3]), haec sunt omnimodis observanda. Primum, sollicitudo rerum carnalium generaliter abscindenda est. Deinde nullius negotii causaeve non solum cura, sed ne memoria quidem penitus admittenda; detra- ctiones, vaniloquia, seu multiloquia, scurrilitates quoque similiter amputandae; irae prae omnibus siv(??) tristitiae perturbatio funditus eruenda; concupiscen- tiae ac philargyriae noxius fomes radicitus evellendus : Et ita his ac similibus vitiis extrusis penitus et abscis- sis, quae hominum quoque possunt patere conspecti- bus, talique, ut diximus, respurgii emendatione prae- missa, quae simplicitatis et innocentiae puritate per- ficitur, jacienda sunt primum profundae humilitatis inconcussa fundamenta, quae scilicet turrim intratu- ram coelos valeant sustinere;
passages.english: But in purity of heart.] Because only the pure in heart will see God. "Now, so that prayer may be sent forth with the fervour and purity with which it ought (so speaks Cassian [Conference 9, ch. 3]), these things must be observed in every way. First, anxiety about fleshly things must be cut off entirely. Next, not only the care but not even the memory of any business or affair must be admitted at all; detractions, idle talk or much talking, and buffoonery likewise must be cut away; above all the disturbance of anger or of sadness must be rooted out completely; the harmful tinder of lust and of avarice (*philargyria*) must be torn up by the roots. And so, when these and similar vices, which can also be open to the sight of men, have been wholly driven out and cut off, and when such a correction by cleansing, as we have said, has gone before, which is accomplished by the purity of simplicity and innocence, there must first be laid the unshakable foundations of deep humility, which may be able to support a tower that is to enter the heavens;
passages.notes: 'siv(??)' read as 'sive' (or).

passages.original: Idem monet vulgatum Syntagma doctrinae S. Athanasii ad monachos : « Per diem frequenter ora, et assidue; attamen sine longa ora- tionis extensione, sine clamore, aut multiloquio mani. » Idque monachorum AEgyptiorum exemplo, qui, ut dicit Cassianus (Lib.ii, cap. 10), utilius censebant breves quidem orationes, sed creberrimas fieri : de quibus etiam S. Augustinus in epistola ad Probam (Epist. 130) : « Dicuntur fratres in AEgypto crebras quidem habere orationes, sed eas tamen brevissimas, et ra- ptim quodammodo jaculatas, ne illa vigilanter erecta, quae oranti plurimum necessaria est, per productio- res moras evanescat atque hebetetur intentio;
passages.english: The well-known *Syntagma of Doctrine* of St Athanasius to monks gives the same advice: "Pray often and constantly during the day; yet without long drawing-out of prayer, without shouting, or empty much-speaking." And this after the example of the Egyptian monks, who, as Cassian says (Book 2, ch. 10), judged it more profitable that prayers be short but very frequent; of whom St Augustine also [writes] in the letter to Proba (Letter 130): "The brethren in Egypt are said to have frequent prayers, but very short ones, and as it were darted out swiftly, lest that alert and upright attention, which is most necessary to one who prays, should fade away and be dulled through longer delays;
passages.notes: 'mani' read as 'inani' (empty, vain).

passages.original: Apua Cassinenses olim unus duntaxat post abbatem erat decanus : et post hunc vicedecanus, ut scribit Nicolaus de Fractura; sed cum Coelestinus papa V suos in Cassinensi monaste- rio introduxisset, « mutavit nomen decani, qui post ipsorum adventum vocatus est pri(??)r, » inquit Richar- dus a Paulo Augustino a Janua citatus ad Regulae c. 55. Et certe in Fossatensi S. Mauri monasterio prio- res etiam appellabantur decani, ut patet ex lib. Mirac. S. Baboleni abbatis c, 5 (Saec.iiBened., p. 595), ubi Robertus ejusdem monasterii modo prior, modo de- canus appellatur.
passages.english: Among the monks of Monte Cassino there was formerly only one dean after the abbot, and after him a vice-dean, as Nicolaus de Fractura writes; but when Pope Celestine V had introduced his own [monks] into the monastery of Monte Cassino, "he changed the name of the dean, who after their arrival was called prior," says Richard, cited by Paulus Augustinus of Genoa on chapter 55 of the Rule. And indeed in the monastery of St Maur-des-Fossés priors were also called deans, as is clear from the book of the *Miracles of St Babolenus the Abbot*, ch. 5 (Second Benedictine Century, p. 595), where Robert of the same monastery is called now prior, now dean.
passages.notes: 'Apua' read as 'Apud'; 'pri(??)r' as 'prior'.

passages.original: » Quem in locum Alardus Gazaeus ita scribit : « Hinc apparet in uno refectorio fuisse distinctas, et divisas fratrum decurias sive decanias; et unicuique decaniae suum assedisse et praesedisse decanum aut decurio- nem; quod et S. Hieronymus indicat ad Eustochium scribens : Unaquaeque, inquit, decuria cum suo pa- rente pergit ad mensam, quibus per singulas hebdo- madas vicissim minist(??)ant. »
passages.english: " On this passage Alardus Gazaeus writes thus: "From this it appears that in one refectory there were distinct and separate decuries or deaneries of brethren, and that its own dean or decurion sat with and presided over each deanery; which St Jerome also indicates, writing to Eustochium: Each decury, he says, goes to table with its own parent, whom they serve in turn week by week."

passages.original: 89) : Si perfectae aetatis sit, decies admoneri ut a vitiis desistat; post haec audire no- lentem monasterii legibus increpari; S. Basilius (Reg. fus., c. 47) : inobedientiae rationem nolentem reddere e fratrum contubernio ejici. Simile aliquid habetur apud Cassianum (Lib.iv, c. 6). Et certe Si quis non obedit verbo nostro per epistolam, inquit Apostolus, hunc notate, et ne commisceamini cum illo (II Thess.iii). Sed S. Columbanus (Poenitentiali) so- lum decernit, ut « si quis frater inobediens fuerit, duos dies unum paximatium et aquam » tantum accipiat.
passages.english: 89): if he is of full age, he is to be admonished ten times to desist from his vices; after this, if he refuses to listen, he is to be rebuked by the laws of the monastery. St Basil (Longer Rules, ch. 47): one who refuses to give an account of his disobedience is to be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. Something similar is found in Cassian (Book 4, ch. 6). And indeed, If anyone does not obey our word by letter, says the Apostle, note that man, and do not associate with him (2 Thess. 3). But St Columbanus (in the Penitential) decrees only that "if any brother is disobedient, he shall receive for two days only one biscuit and water."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference (Pachomius, article 89).

passages.original: » Joanni Craesbeeck, quem nec opprobria, nec animae peri- cula movent. Joannes de Précis abbas S. Germani Parisiensis hunc locum Gallice ita reddit : S'il ne l'entend, et est rebelle. Versio ms. S. Petri Conchen- sis : S'il est obstiné. Versio Guidonis Juvenalis : S'il est deshonté ne tenant conte de cela. Recentiores : S'il est endurci.
passages.english: " To Joannes Craesbeeck, [he is one] whom neither reproaches nor dangers to the soul move. Joannes de Précis, abbot of Saint-Germain at Paris, renders this place in French thus: 'If he does not heed it, and is rebellious.' The manuscript version of Saint-Pierre de Conches: 'If he is obstinate.' The version of Guido Juvenalis: 'If he is shameless, taking no account of that.' More recent [versions]: 'If he is hardened.'
passages.notes: French quotations translated.

passages.original: qui seniori inobediens fuerit, qui contumaciter seniori responderit, qui erga seniorum linguam non represserit, qui lascivus in lingua fuerit, qui inhoneste incesserit, qui jocaverit, qui satis riserit, qui cum excommunicato locutus fuerit, oraverit, aut comederit; qui illusionem no- cturnam Patri non patefecerit, haec igitur et similia triduana excommunicatione emendanda sunt. » His fere similia sunt ea quae refert Cassianus I. iv, cap. 16.
passages.english: whoever is disobedient to a senior, whoever answers a senior insolently, whoever has not restrained his tongue toward seniors, whoever is wanton in speech, whoever walks about indecently, whoever jokes, whoever laughs too much, whoever speaks, prays, or eats with an excommunicated person; whoever has not disclosed a nocturnal illusion to the Father — these things, then, and the like are to be corrected by a three-day excommunication." Almost similar to these are the things Cassian relates, book 4, ch. 16.

passages.original: De poenis quibus excommunicati pro gravioribus culpis plecterentur dicturis ante videtur inquirendum quaenam graviores poenae censeri debeant. Et quidem eo in numero primum reponi posse eas existimo quas veteres monachi plagis emendabant, aut expulsione purgabant, quasque refert Cassianus his verbis (Lib.iv, cap. 16) : « Residua vero quae apud nos indiffe- renter admissa, a nobis quoque reprehensibilius sus- tinentur; id est aperta convicia, manifesti contem- ptus, contradictiones tumidae, libera et effrenata pro- cessio, familiaritas apud feminas, irae, rixae, simul- tates, et jurgia, operis peculiaris praesumptio; phi- largyriae contagio, affectus atque possessio rerum su- perfluarum, quae a caeteris fratribus non habentur, extraordinaria ac furtiva cibi refectio, et his similia, non illa increpatione quam diximus, spiritali;
passages.english: As we are about to speak of the penalties with which the excommunicated were punished for graver faults, it seems we must first ask which faults ought to be judged graver. And indeed I think that in that number may first be placed those which the ancient monks corrected with blows or purged by expulsion, and which Cassian relates in these words (Book 4, ch. 16): "But the remaining [faults], which among us are committed indiscriminately, are treated by them also as more reprehensible: that is, open insults, manifest contempt, swollen contradictions, free and unbridled going out, familiarity with women, anger, quarrels, grudges and disputes, presumption in private work, the contagion of avarice, the desire for and possession of superfluous things which the other brethren do not have, extraordinary and stealthy eating of food, and the like, [are corrected] not by that spiritual rebuke which we mentioned;
passages.notes: 'a nobis' (by us) seems to stand for 'ab illis'/'apud eos' in Cassian's sense; translated as 'by them' for coherence.

passages.original: Si quis frater praesumpserit sine jussione abbatis fratri excommunicato quolibet modo se jungere, aut loqui cum eo, vel mandatum ei c dirigere, similem sor- tiatur excommunicationis vindictam.] Quod ex antiqua veterum monachorum disciplina desumpsit, apud quos, « si quis, ut ait Cassianus (Lib.ii, cap. 16), pro ad- misso quolibet delicto fuerit ab oratione suspensus, nullus cum eo prorsus orandi habet licentiam, ante- quam submissa in terram poenitentia reconciliatio ejus, et admissi venia coram fratribus cunctis publice fuerit ab abbate concessa; ob hoc namque tali obser- vantia semetipsos ab orationis ejus consortio segre- gant atque secernunt, quod credum eum qui ab ora- tione suspenditur, secundum Apostoli sententiam tradi Satanae; et si quis orationi ejus antequam re- cipiatur a seniore inconsiderata pietate permotus communicare.375 praesumpserit, complicem se damnationis ejus efficiat, tradens scilicet semetipsum voluntarie Satanae, cui ille pro sui reatus emenda- tione fuerat deputat(??)s, in eo vel maxime gravius crimen incurrens, quod cum illo se vel confabula- tionis, vel orationis communione miscendo, majorem illi generet insolentiae fomitem, et contumaciam de- linquentis in pejus enutriat.
passages.english: If any brother presumes, without the abbot's order, to associate in any way with an excommunicated brother, or to speak with him, or to send him a message, let him receive a like punishment of excommunication.] This he took from the ancient discipline of the old monks, among whom, "if anyone," as Cassian says (Book II, ch. 16), "has been suspended from prayer for any offence committed, no one at all has leave to pray with him until, after penance done lying on the ground, his reconciliation and pardon for what he committed has been publicly granted by the abbot before all the brothers; for they separate and set themselves apart from fellowship in his prayer by such an observance for this reason, that they believe that he who is suspended from prayer is, according to the Apostle's judgement, handed over to Satan; and if anyone, moved by thoughtless compassion, presumes to share in his prayer before he is received back by the elder, he makes himself an accomplice of his condemnation, namely by voluntarily handing himself over to Satan, to whom that man had been assigned for the correction of his guilt; and in this especially he incurs a graver crime, that by mixing with him in the fellowship either of conversation or of prayer he gives him greater fuel for insolence and nourishes the offender's obstinacy for the worse."
passages.notes: "credum" read as "credunt"; "deputat(??)s" as "deputatus"; "375" is a page number, omitted. The opening is the lemma of the Rule being commented on.

passages.original: ] Radicitus, id est a corde, quod est fons, radix, et 422 origo omnis mali omnisque cupiditatis; « ut nec in intentione, nec in voluntate remanent aliquid de proprietate, per quod possit ad actum aliquem pullulare, » inquit Bernardus Cassin. Et recte omni- no : nam, ut ait Cassianus, « non solum pecuniarum est cavenda possessio, verum etiam voluntas ipsa ab animo penitus extrudenda : non enim tam effectus philargyriae vitandus est. quam affectus ipsius radici- tus amputandus est; nihil enim proderit pecunias non habere, si voluntas in nobis fuerit possidendi. » Ve- rum non solum voluntas desideriumque habendi, sed etiam vel minimus, in his quae nobis ad usum conce- duntur, affectus resecandus est.
passages.english: ] "At the root," that is, from the heart, which is the fount, root and origin of all evil and of all greed; "so that nothing of ownership remains either in intention or in will, through which it could sprout into any act," says Bernard of Monte Cassino. And quite rightly: for, as Cassian says, "not only must the possession of money be guarded against, but also the very wish [for it] must be driven out of the mind entirely; for it is not so much the effect of avarice (*philargyria*) that is to be avoided as its disposition that is to be cut off at the root; for it will profit nothing not to have money if the will to possess is in us." But not only the will and desire of having, but even the least attachment to the things granted us for use must be cut away.
passages.notes: "422" is a page number, omitted. "remanent" taken as "remaneat".

passages.original: monach.) : « Ministerium in communi conventu alternis vieibus fiat, duo secun- dum ordinem in hehdomada una omne studium ad usum requisitum expleant. » Apud S. Hieronymum in praefatione ad Regulam S Pachomii : « in hebdo- madarum ministerio sibi su cedant per ordinem. » Apud Cassianum (Lib.iv, c. 19): « Per cunctam namque Mesopotamiam, Palaestinam, et Cappado- ciam, ac totum Orientem, singulis hebdomadibus vi- cissim fratres ad haec officia sibi reddenda suceedunt. ita ut secundum coenobii multitudinem ministrorum quoque numerus deputetur. » Denique in Vita S Ma- riani ad S. Germanum Autissiodoreusem monachi, saeculo v, ad quem Olinitius i em monachus dixisse fertur : « Sors mea est ad me sam fratribus mini- strare et alimoniam parare.
passages.english: monks): "Let service in the common community be done by turns; let two in order fulfil in one week all the work required for use." In St Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of St Pachomius: "in the service of the weeks let them succeed one another in order." In Cassian (Book IV, ch. 19): "For throughout all Mesopotamia, Palestine and Cappadocia, and the whole East, the brothers succeed one another in turn each week in rendering these duties, so that the number of servers too is assigned according to the size of the monastery." Finally, in the Life of St Marianus, monk under St Germanus of Auxerre, in the fifth century, to whom Olinitius, a monk likewise, is said to have said: "It is my lot to serve the brothers and prepare food."
passages.notes: Passage begins mid-citation (Basil, Sermon on the Institution of Monks). Name "Olinitius" unidentified; "i em" read as "item"; "me sam" uncertain, perhaps "mensam" ("to serve the brothers at table").

passages.original: Postulantes pro se orari.] Idem post coenam conve- nientes in unum ad concinendos ex more ante quie- tem hymnos, praestabant in Oriente veteres monachi, quemadmodum scribit Cassianus (Lib.iv, c. 19).
passages.english: Asking to be prayed for.] The ancient monks in the East did the same when gathering together after supper to sing hymns together before rest, as was the custom, as Cassian writes (Book IV, ch. 19).

passages.original: Atque ita placuit pri- scis vitae monasticae Patribus, ut videre est in Regula S. Pachomii art. 20; S. Caesarii ad virgines, cap. 30; S. Aureliani ad monachos cap. 53, et ad virgines cap. 37; Cujusdam etiam ad virgines cap. 15, apud Hieronymum epist. 22, in concil. Agathensi cap. 38, et in Vita S. Eugendi abbatis Jurensis apud Boll. 1 Januar.
passages.english: And so it pleased the early Fathers of monastic life, as may be seen in the Rule of St Pachomius, art. 20; of St Caesarius for virgins, ch. 30; of St Aurelian for monks, ch. 53, and for virgins, ch. 37; also of a certain [author] for virgins, ch. 15; in Jerome, Letter 22; in the Council of Agde, ch. 38; and in the Life of St Eugendus, abbot of Jura, in the Bollandists, 1 January.

passages.original: Et Cistercienses : « Si quae vero moniales ad balnea extra monasteria processerint, irremissibiliter pri- ventur habitu regulari : licentiantes autem ut prae- dicta petant balnea, sententiam excommunicationis incurrant. » Huicce statuto occasionem forte dederit S. Hieronymus ad Laetam scribens in haec verba (Epist. 7) : « Mihi omnino in adulta virgine lavacra displicent, quae seipsam debet erubescere, et nudam videre non posse; si enim vigiliis et jejuniis macerat corpus suum, et in servitutem redigit, si flammas libidinis, et incentiva ferventis aetatis exstinguere cupit continentiae frigore, si appetitis sordibus tur- pare festinat naturatem pulchritudinem, cur econ- trario balnearum fomentis sopitos ignes suscitat?
passages.english: And the Cistercians: "If any nuns go out to baths outside the monasteries, let them be deprived irremissibly of the regular habit; and those who give them leave to go to the said baths shall incur the sentence of excommunication." Occasion for this statute was perhaps given by St Jerome writing to Laeta in these words (Letter 7): "For my part, I entirely disapprove of baths for a grown virgin, who ought to blush at herself and be unable to see herself naked; for if she wastes her body with vigils and fasts and brings it into subjection, if she desires to extinguish the flames of lust and the incitements of hot youth with the coldness of continence, if she hastens to disfigure her natural beauty with deliberate squalor, why on the contrary does she rouse the slumbering fires with the warmth of baths?"
passages.notes: "naturatem" read as "naturalem".

passages.original: Istud tamen ad mensam silentium ita observabant veteres, ut ex Cassiano licitum esset decano loqui; ex Regula secunda et tertia SS. Patrum, cap. 7, atque S. Macarii, cap. 18, ei qui praeest; ex Regula S. Be- nedicti, priori pro aedificatione; ex Poenitentiali S.
passages.english: This silence at table, however, the ancients observed in such a way that, according to Cassian, the dean was allowed to speak; according to the second and third Rule of the Holy Fathers, ch. 7, and that of St Macarius, ch. 18, the one presiding; according to the Rule of St Benedict, the prior, for edification; according to the Penitential of St
passages.notes: Sentence breaks off; continues "Columbanus, everyone for the need of another brother".

passages.original: Conchensi propter communionem ita reddit : Pour la sainte communion, c'est-à dire pour le corps de nostre Seigneur, que l'en seult recevoir à la messe, Expositio Theobaldi Artaldi Coelestini : Pour la sainte communion, que le liseur a reçû na- gueres en la messe, etc. Versio Guidonis Juvenalis : Pour la sainte communion, qu'il a reçuë, afin qu'il ne demeure rien entre les dents ou ailleurs, qu'on peut gecter en lisant pour les fleumes qui viennent. Exposi- tio Matthiae Lamberti : A cause de la sainte commu- nion, de peur qu'en crachant il advienne quolque irre- verance à icelle pour les flegmes qu'il pourroit jetter en lisant.
passages.english: from Conches renders "propter communionem" thus: "For the holy communion, that is, for the body of our Lord, which one is accustomed to receive at Mass." The exposition of Theobald Artaud, Celestine: "For the holy communion which the reader received shortly before at Mass, etc." The version of Guy Juvenal: "For the holy communion which he has received, so that nothing remains between the teeth or elsewhere which might be spat out while reading because of the phlegm that comes." The exposition of Matthias Lambert: "Because of the holy communion, lest in spitting some irreverence happen to it because of the phlegm he might cast out while reading."
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ("An old [version] from a manuscript of Conches"). French quotations translated into English.

passages.original: 517 Primo, quod S. P. Benedictus veteres mo- nachos in multis seculus duces, tum hac in parte satis probabiliter aemulatus est. Porro de illis ita discurrit apud Cassianum abbas Moyses (Collat. 2, cap. 19) : « Discutientes continentias diversorum, qui vel solis leguminibus, vel oleribus tantum, vel pomis vitam jugiter exigebant, praeposuere cu(??)ctis illis refectionem solius panis, cujus aequissimum mo- dum in duobus paximatiis statuerunt, quos parvulos panes vix librae unius pondus habere certissimum est. » Hanc libram fuisse unciarum duodecim colli- gitur ex paximatiorum pondere, quod sex unciis constitisse patet ex Palladio, qui agens de Paulo Simplice sic habet : « Fert Antonius et imponit mensae quatuor paxamidia sex unciarum, et sibi qui- dem unum madefecit.
passages.english: First, that our holy father Benedict, having followed the ancient monks as guides in many things, also imitated them quite probably in this respect. Now concerning them Abbot Moses discourses thus in Cassian (Conference 2, ch. 19): "Examining the abstinences of various men who spent their life continually on pulses alone, or on vegetables only, or on fruit, they preferred to all these the meal of bread alone, whose most fitting measure they fixed at two paximatia, small loaves which it is quite certain scarcely weigh one pound." That this pound was of twelve ounces is gathered from the weight of the paximatia, which plainly was six ounces, from Palladius, who, treating of Paul the Simple, says: "Antony brings and sets on the table four paxamidia of six ounces, and moistened one for himself."
passages.notes: "517" page number omitted; "seculus" read as "secutus". *Paximatia* are small dried loaves (biscuits).

passages.original: Et ideo cum aliqua scrupulositate a nobit mensura victus aliorum constituitur.] Eamdem difficultatem olim expertus est Cassianus, uti ipse testatur in lib. v, cap. 5.
passages.english: And therefore it is with some scruple that the measure of others' food is set down by us.] Cassian once experienced the same difficulty, as he himself testifies in Book V, ch. 5.
passages.notes: "nobit" read as "nobis".

passages.original: 22) : « De cibo, inquit, et potu taceo, cum ibi etiam languentes monachi aqua utantur fri- gida, et coctum aliquid accepisse luxuria sit. » Me- nardus etiam dictum ascribit abbati Pastori, uti nar- ratur in lib. iv de Vit. Pat., n. 31, interprete Pelagio. Quamvis an ita revera se res habeat dubitaverint non- nulli, eo quod probabile non videatur hunc librum a Pelagio translatum fuisse ante annum 537, quo in Palaestina et Oriente legationem obibat : quo tempore suam sanctus Benedictus scripserat Regulam.
passages.english: 22): "I say nothing," he says, "of food and drink, since there even sick monks use cold water, and to have taken anything cooked is [counted] luxury." Ménard also ascribes the saying to Abbot Pastor (Poemen), as is narrated in book 4 of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 31, in the translation of Pelagius. Some, however, have doubted whether this is really so, because it does not seem probable that this book was translated by Pelagius before the year 537, when he was undertaking an embassy in Palestine and the East; by which time St. Benedict had written his Rule.
passages.notes: The opening "22)" completes a reference to Jerome's letter to Eustochium (Epist. 22) begun in the preceding context. "Menardus" is taken to be Hugues Ménard, the Maurist editor; "abbas Pastor" is the Latin name of the Desert Father Poemen.

passages.original: Benedictus toto tempore Paschali praescribit jejunium, idque juxta antiquum Ecclesiae morem, quo a Pascha ad Pentecosten, ob reverentiam domi- nicae Resurrectionis, jejunium solvebatur, ut videre est apud Tertullianum, lib. de Corona militis; san- ctum Epiphanium, in Compend. doct. Eccles.; S. Augustinum epist. 55; Regulam Magistri, c. 28: Haymonem Halberstatensem, lib. i de Variet., cap. 14. Quae consuetudo pariter apud monachos commu- niter viguit, ut patet ex Cassiano, lib.
passages.english: Benedict prescribes [no] fast during the whole of Eastertide, and this according to the ancient custom of the Church, by which from Easter to Pentecost, out of reverence for the Lord's Resurrection, fasting was suspended, as can be seen in Tertullian, in the book On the Soldier's Crown; Saint Epiphanius, in the Compendium of Church Doctrine; Saint Augustine, letter 55; the Rule of the Master, chapter 28; Haymo of Halberstadt, book 1 On Varieties, chapter 14. This custom likewise prevailed generally among monks, as is clear from Cassian, book
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence: the context before reads 'Nullum ergo S. P.', so the sense is 'Our holy Father Benedict therefore prescribes no fast'. 'Nullum' is supplied in brackets. The final citation continues into the following context.

passages.original: » Eadem ratione sanctus Maglorius (In ejus Vita, saec.iBened.) « in quarta feria et sexta ab om- nium ciborum pabulo exstitit alienus, quam obser- vationem jejunii in quarta feria explevit, eo quod in ea sacrilegi et rei facti Judaei sanguineum, ut aucto- rem suum Dominum morti traderent, pactum sta- fuerunt : sexta autem feria, quia id quod de corde conceperant, ipsum cruci affigentes, in hac opere compleverunt. » Eamdem etiam rationem profert sanctus Augustinus ad Casulanum scribens, et Ri- chardus de S. Angelo in hunc locum. Verumtamen Hildemarus adhuc altius hujus consuetudinis origi- nem repetens : « Haec, inquit, consuetudo jejunandi quarta feria et sexta feria, orta est a sanctis Patri- bus, nec non et Judaica fuit, sicut Pha- risaeus dicit : Jejuno bis in sabbato.
passages.english: " For the same reason Saint Magloire (in his Life, first Benedictine century) "on the fourth and sixth weekdays abstained from the nourishment of all foods.
