He kept this observance of fasting on the fourth weekday because on it the Jews, made sacrilegious and guilty, settled the bloody compact to hand over their Author, the Lord, to death; and on the sixth weekday because on it they carried out in deed what they had conceived in their heart, fixing him to the cross." Saint Augustine too gives the same reason, writing to Casulanus, and so does Richard of Sant'Angelo on this passage. Hildemar, however, traces the origin of this custom still further back: "This custom," he says, "of fasting on the fourth weekday and the sixth weekday arose from the holy Fathers, and was also Jewish, as the Pharisee says: I fast twice in the week."
passages.notes: The opening quotation mark closes a quotation that began in the preceding context. 'Saec. i Bened.' probably refers to the first century of the Acta Sanctorum O.S.B. 'Sabbato' here means 'week', following the Gospel idiom.

passages.original: Neque tamen de(??)uerunt ex priscis monachis qui prandium ad sextam, et sero coenam aestate sibi pa- rarent, quod de Tabennensibus imprimis refert san- ctus Hieronymus (Praefat. ad Regulam S. Pachomii): « Bis, inquit, in hebdomada die quarta et sexta sab- bati ab omnibus jejunatur, excepta Pentecoste : aliis diebus comedunt, qui volunt post meridiem, et in coena similiter mensa ponitur propter laborantes, senes, pueros, et aestus gravissimos. Sunt qui secundo parum comedunt, alii qui prandii sive coenae uno tan- tum cibo contenti sunt, nonnulli gustato paululum pane egrediuntur.
passages.english: Yet there were some among the early monks who in summer provided themselves with a midday meal at the sixth hour and a supper in the evening. Saint Jerome reports this especially of the Tabennesiots (Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius): "Twice in the week," he says, "on the fourth and sixth day of the week, all fast, except at Pentecost. On other days those who wish eat after midday, and at supper likewise a table is set, for the sake of those who labour, the old, the boys, and in the most severe heat. There are some who eat little the second time, others who are content with a single dish at either the midday meal or supper, and some who go out after tasting a little bread."
passages.notes: 'de(??)uerunt' is read as 'defuerunt'.

passages.original: Non autem Eptaticum aut Requm.] « Heptateucus, inquit sanctus Augustinus (Lib.iide Doct. Christ. cap. 8), continet quinque libros Mosis, librum Josue, et Judicum : nam quod spectat ad librum Roth, ma- gis ad Regnorum principia videtur pertinere. »
passages.english: But not the Heptateuch or Kings.] "The Heptateuch," says Saint Augustine (On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8), "contains the five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, and Judges; for as for the book of Ruth, it seems rather to belong to the beginnings of Kingdoms."
passages.notes: 'Requm' is read as 'Regum'. 'Roth' is read as 'Ruth'.

passages.original: Bernardus tamen videtur sentire in glossa praece- denti, quod hujusmodi 581 satisfactio publica sit illa chori communis separatio. Ni olaus tamen dicit, quod circa ultimam orationem hujusmodi officii fra- ter reus debet jacere prostratus in medio dicti pavi- menti, donec conventus ab oratorio exiverit. Idem dicit Cassianus, ut notat hic Smaragdus, et hoc credo verius. In meo tamen monasterio consueverunt se- niores tarde ad oratorium occurrentes, vel in aliquo ibi fallentes, statim ibidem flectere genua; et in hoc reputantur satisfecisse;
passages.english: Bernard, however, seems to hold in the preceding gloss that public satisfaction of this kind is that common separation from the choir. Nicholas, however, says that around the last prayer of this office the guilty brother must lie prostrate in the middle of the said floor until the community has gone out of the oratory. Cassian says the same, as Smaragdus notes here, and this I believe is more correct. In my monastery, however, the seniors who come late to the oratory, or make some mistake there, have been accustomed to kneel immediately on the spot, and by this they are considered to have made satisfaction;
passages.notes: 'Ni olaus' is read as 'Nicolaus'. The number 581 is a page number and is omitted.

passages.original: Nec quisquam praesumat ante statutam horam vel postea quidquam cibi vel potus percipere.] Haec fuit ge- neralis omnium veterum monachorum praxis, quam videre est, tum apud Cassianum, tum in omnibus eorum Regulis : « Antequam vel postquam legitimam communemque refectionem percipiant, inquit Cas- sianus (Lib.iv, cap. 18), summa cautione servatur ne extra mensam quioquam cibi potusve ori suo quis- quam indulgere praesumat; ut incedentibus per hor- los et pomaria, cum passim blandeque per arbores poma pendentia non solum se objiciant pectoribus transeuntium, verum etiam strata per terram con- culcanda pedibus se offerant, atque ad colligendum parata facile ad consensum concupiscentiae illicere valeant intuentes, et opportunitate ac copia quamvis districtos atque abstinentissimos ad sui desiderlum provocare;
passages.english: And let no one presume to take any food or drink before or after the appointed hour.] This was the general practice of all the ancient monks, as can be seen both in Cassian and in all their Rules. "Before or after they take the lawful and common meal," says Cassian (book 4, chapter 18), "the greatest care is taken that no one presume to indulge his mouth with any food or drink away from the table. So, as they walk through gardens and orchards, the fruits hanging everywhere and enticingly on the trees not only thrust themselves before the chests of those passing by, but also offer themselves strewn on the ground to be trampled underfoot. Ready to be gathered, they could easily lure the onlookers into consenting to desire, and by the opportunity and abundance provoke even the strict and most abstinent to desire them;
passages.notes: 'horlos' is read as 'hortos', 'quioquam' as 'quidquam', and 'desiderlum' as 'desiderium'. The sentence continues into the following context.

passages.original: Benedictum de excommunicatione ecclesiastica locutum fuisse cap. 25 existimat. Similem pene poenam in negligen- tes tardeque venientes ad opus Dei statuerant anti- qui Mesopotamiae monachi; si quis enim in eam incurrisset culpam, is, teste Cassiano (Lib.iii, c. 7), « Oratorium introire non audebat, nec semetipsum admiscere psallentibus; sed congregationis missam stans pro foribus praestolabatur, donec egredientibus cunctis, submissa in terram poenitentia, negligentiae suae vel tarditatis impetraret veniam. » Quamvis non a solis priscis monachis id poenitentiae genus acce- perit S.
passages.english: [...] thinks that Benedict spoke of ecclesiastical excommunication in chapter 25. The ancient monks of Mesopotamia had laid down an almost similar penalty for those who were negligent and came late to the Work of God. For if anyone incurred that fault, he, as Cassian testifies (book 3, chapter 7), "did not dare enter the oratory, nor mingle with those singing psalms; but standing before the doors he awaited the dismissal of the community, until, as all came out, he obtained pardon for his negligence or lateness by prostrating himself to the ground in penance." Yet Saint Benedict did not receive this kind of penance from the early monks alone,
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. The context before gives 'which confirms the opinion which S.', so the subject is probably someone named 'S.' (a saint) whose name is cut off. The sentence also ends mid-way, with 'Benedictus' in the following context; 'S.' is rendered there as 'Saint'.

passages.original: nisi cum sa- tisfactione ibi coram omnibus humiliatus fuerit, etc.] Qualis esse debeat humilitatis satisfactio qua de hoc capite, S. Pater non satis aperit. Ei quidem veteres Aegypti Tabennensesque monachi eum gravi plecte- bant vindicta, qui decantans psalmum vel modicum titubaret; nam, ut scribit Cassianus (Lib.iv, cap. 16), « non aliter negligentiam suam quam publica diluebat poenitentia; cunctisque in synaxi fratribus congregatis, tandiu prostratus in terra veniam postu- labat, donec orationum consummaretur solemnitas, impetraturus eam, cum jussus fuisset abbatis judicio de solo surgere. » S. Columbanus (In Poeniten.) vult ut « qui ob tussim in exordio psalmi non bene can- taverit, sex 596 percussionibus emendare statua- tur.
passages.english: unless he has been humbled there before all with satisfaction, etc.] What the satisfaction of humility on this point ought to be, the holy Father does not make sufficiently clear. The ancient monks of Egypt and Tabennesi indeed punished with a heavy penalty anyone who stumbled even slightly while chanting a psalm. For, as Cassian writes (book 4, chapter 16), "he washed away his negligence only by public penance: with all the brothers gathered in the synaxis, he lay prostrate on the ground asking pardon until the solemnity of the prayers was completed, and was to obtain it when he was ordered by the abbot's judgement to rise from the ground." Saint Columban (in the Penitential) wishes that "one who, because of a cough, has not sung well at the beginning of a psalm, should be appointed to make amends with six blows."
passages.notes: 'Ei quidem' is probably a scanning error for 'Et quidem'. The number 596 is a page number and is omitted. 'Synaxis' means the assembly for prayer.

passages.original: 599Aut fregerit quidpiam.] Quanta severitate ve- teres monachi eos plecterent qui aliquid fregissent docet Cassianus his verbis (Lib.iv, cap. 16): « Si quis gillonem fictilem, quem baucalem nuncupant, casu aliquo fregerit, non aliter negligentiam suam quam publica diluet poenitentia; cunctisque in synaxi fratribus congregatis, tandiu prostratus in terram veniam postulabit, donec orationum consummetur solemnitas, impetraturus eam cum jussus fuerit ab- batis judicio de solo surgere. » In Regula tamen S. Pachomii (Art. 70) solum decernitur, ut « si quis vas fictile fregerit, vel aliquam utilem rem ad usus monasterii, agat poenitentiam.» Sed Regula Magistri (Cap.
passages.english: Or has broken something.] Cassian shows how severely the ancient monks punished those who had broken something, in these words (book 4, chapter 16): "If anyone by some accident has broken an earthenware jar, which they call a *baucalis*, he will wash away his negligence only by public penance: with all the brothers gathered in the synaxis, he will ask pardon lying prostrate on the ground until the solemnity of the prayers is completed, and will obtain it when he is ordered by the abbot's judgement to rise from the ground." In the Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 70), however, it is only decreed that "if anyone breaks an earthenware vessel, or any useful thing for the use of the monastery, he should do penance." But the Rule of the Master (chapter
passages.notes: '599' at the start is a page number and is omitted. The chapter number of the Rule of the Master continues into the following context.

passages.original: Vel aliud quid excesserit.] Ut sunt ea quae etiam describit Cassianus his verbis (Lib.iv, cap. 16): « Quisquis ad opus aliquod aecersitus, vel ad con- gregationem solitam tardius occurrerit, aut si de- cantans psalmum, vel modicum titubaverit; similiter si superflue, si durius, si contumacius responderit, si negligentius obsequia injuncta compleverit, si vel leviter murmuraverit, si lectionem operi vel obedien- tiae praeferens officia statuta segnius fuerit exsecutus, si dimissa synaxi non concitus ad cellam recurrere festinaverit, si cum aliquo vel ad modicum substi- terit, vel si ad punctum temporis uspiam secesserit, si alterius tenuerit manum, si cum illo qui cellulae suae cohabitator non est, confabulari quantulumcun- que praesumpserit, si oraverit cum illo 600 qui est ab oratione suspensus, si parentum quempiam vel amicorum saecularium videriti, vel collocutus eis sine suo fuerit seniore, si epistolam cujuscunque suscipere, si rescribere sine abbate suo tentaverit.
passages.english: Or has committed some other fault.] Such as those which Cassian also describes in these words (book 4, chapter 16): "Whoever, when summoned to some work or to the usual assembly, comes too late; or if, while chanting a psalm, he stumbles even slightly; likewise if he answers needlessly, harshly, or insolently; if he carries out the tasks enjoined on him rather carelessly; if he murmurs even slightly; if, preferring reading to work or obedience, he performs the appointed duties sluggishly; if, when the synaxis is dismissed, he does not hurry back promptly to his cell; if he stops with anyone even for a little while; or if he withdraws anywhere for a moment of time; if he holds another's hand; if he presumes to chat even a little with one who is not the co-dweller of his cell; if he prays with one who is suspended from prayer; if he sees any of his relatives or worldly friends, or speaks with them without his senior; if he attempts to receive a letter from anyone, or to write back, without his abbot."
passages.notes: 'aecersitus' is read as 'accersitus', and 'videriti' as 'viderit'. The number 600 is a page number and is omitted.

passages.original: 71), « ut quando fratres aestivo tempore jejunant, post sextam dormiant: » testaturque Petrus Venerabilis (Stat. 25), quod « antiquus monachorum mos erat jejuniorum diebus detrimenti usitati somni con- gruenti dormitione ante mensam compensare : unde Hieronymus : Saepe vacuo ventre dormiendum est. » Et in Regula Magistri legitur (Cap. 50) : « Statim post sextam tam post prandium quam in jejunio omnes modice in suis lectis meridientur. » Atque ita Cistercienses in lib.
passages.english: 71), "that when the brothers fast in the summer season, they should sleep after Sext"; and Peter the Venerable testifies (Statute 25) that "it was the ancient custom of monks on fast days to make up for the loss of their accustomed sleep by a fitting sleep before the meal; hence Jerome: One must often sleep on an empty stomach." And in the Rule of the Master one reads (Chapter 50): "Immediately after Sext, both after the midday meal and on a fast, let all take a moderate midday rest in their beds." And so the Cistercians in the Book
passages.notes: The passage begins and ends mid-sentence: the opening "71)" completes a canon reference to the Synod of Aachen from the preceding context, and "in lib." continues as "Book of Usages" (Liber Usuum) in the following context.

passages.original: Aliis expellendo otio, ac pietati fovendae perop- portunum visum est libros scribere; quem laborem imprimis commendat Cassiodorus ad monachos suos sic scribens (De Institui. divin. Scrip., cap. 30) : « Ego fateor votum meum inter vos : quaecunque possunt corporeo labore compleri, antiquariorum studia (si tamen veraciter scribant) non immerito forsitan plus placere, quod et mentem suam relegendo Scripturas divinas salubriter instruant, et Domini praecepta scribendo longe lateque disseminent, felix intentio, laudanda sedulitas, manu hominibus praedi- care, digitis linguas aperire, salutem mortalibus taci- tam dare, et contra diaboli subreptiones illicitas ca- lamo atramentoque pugnare : tot enim vulnera Sata- nas accipit quot antiquarius Domini verba describit.
passages.english: To others it seemed very fitting, for driving out idleness and fostering piety, to copy books. Cassiodorus especially commends this labour, writing thus to his monks (On the Institutes of Divine Scripture, chapter 30): "I confess my wish among you: of all the things that can be accomplished by bodily labour, the pursuits of the copyists (provided they copy accurately) perhaps not undeservedly please [me] more, because by rereading the divine Scriptures they wholesomely instruct their own minds, and by writing they spread the Lord's precepts far and wide. A happy aim, a praiseworthy diligence: to preach to men with the hand, to open tongues with the fingers, to give silent salvation to mortals, and to fight with pen and ink against the unlawful stealthy attacks of the devil. For Satan receives as many wounds as the copyist writes out words of the Lord."

passages.original: Sexto, quia scientia inflat, ut ait Apostolus, nec sine aliquo animi dolore videre possumus viros do- ctos, sui ipsius ignaros, depecta humili professionis suae conditione, honores ambire, cathedras concio- natorum aucupari, extra metas status sui foras pro- dire: quod utinam non ita frequens experiremur! At vero labor manuum fastus vitae praeteritae et delicia- rum facit oblivisci, et humilitatem cordis contritione corporis acquirit, ut docet inter alios Cassianus.
passages.english: Sixth, because knowledge puffs up, as the Apostle says, and we cannot see without some grief of mind learned men, ignorant of themselves, scorning the humble condition of their profession, canvassing for honours, hunting after preachers' pulpits, going out beyond the bounds of their state: would that we did not experience this so often! But manual labour makes one forget the pride and pleasures of one's past life, and acquires humility of heart through the mortification of the body, as Cassian among others teaches.
passages.notes: "depecta" read as "despecta" (scorned).

passages.original: Eodem tempore vivebat alter Ammonius, abbatis Pambo discipulus, vir insigniter doctus (Pallad. in Laus., c. 12), qui « Vetus et Novum Testamentum dicebat memoriter, et in doctorum virorum Origenis, et Didymi, et Pierii, et Stephani scriptis ita erat ver- satus, ut sexagies centena millia versuum percurre- rit. » Hic magno Athanasio Romam proficiscenti da- tus est socius, vir, teste Socrate (Lib.iv, cap. 18), adeo « parum curiosus, ut cum Romae una cum Atha- nasio forte versaretur, nihil ex magnificis urbis ope- ribus, praeter templum Petro et Paulo dicatum, videre omnino desideraret.
passages.english: At the same time there lived another Ammonius, a disciple of Abbot Pambo, a remarkably learned man (Palladius, Lausiac History, ch. 12), who "recited the Old and New Testament from memory, and was so versed in the writings of the learned men Origen, Didymus, Pierius and Stephen that he had gone through six million lines." He was given as a companion to the great Athanasius when he set out for Rome, a man, as Socrates testifies (Book 4, ch. 18), so "little given to curiosity that when he happened to be staying in Rome together with Athanasius, he had no desire at all to see anything of the city's magnificent works except the church dedicated to Peter and Paul.
passages.notes: The quotation closes in the following context. "sexagies centena millia" is literally sixty times a hundred thousand, i.e. six million lines.

passages.original: » Adeo verum est, quod aiunt nonnulli, scientiam in monachis parere curiositatem, cosque ad curas externas plus aequo effundere. Eo- dem referri debet quod de Theone abbate, qui tri- ginta annis in domuncula seorsum inclusus silentium exercuit, tradunt Rufinus (Ruf. lib.iide Vit. Patr. cap. 6) et Palladius (Pall. Laus. cap. 50), quod scili- cet « erat vir eruditus in triplici gratia sermonum, in scriptis Romanis, Graecis et Aegyptiacis. »
passages.english: So true is what some say, that learning in monks breeds curiosity and pours them out more than is right into external cares. To the same point should be referred what Rufinus (Rufinus, Lives of the Fathers, book 2, chapter 6) and Palladius (Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 50) relate of the abbot Theon, who, shut up apart in a little dwelling for thirty years, practised silence: namely that "he was a learned man in a threefold grace of languages, in Roman, Greek and Egyptian writings."
passages.notes: "cosque" read as "eosque".

passages.original: 4): « Dum essem, inquit, juvenis, et solitudinis me deserta vallarent, incentiva vitiorum, ardoremque naturae ferre non po- teram; quem cum crebris jejuniis frangerem, meus tamen cogitationibus aestuabat. Ad quam edomandam cuidam fratri, qui ex Hebraeis crediderat, me in di- sciplinam dedi; ut post Quintiliani acumina, Cicero- nis fluvios, gravitatemque Frontonis, et lenitatem Plinii, alphabetum discerem, et stridentia anhelan- tiaque verba meditarer. Quid ibi laboris insumpse- rim, quid sustinucrim difficultatis, quoties desperave- rim, quoties cessaverim, et contentione discendi rur- sus incoeperim;
passages.english: 4): "When I was young," he says, "and the deserts of solitude walled me in, I could not bear the incitements of the vices and the heat of nature; and though I broke it with frequent fasts, my mind nonetheless seethed with thoughts. To subdue it I gave myself as a pupil to a certain brother who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, so that after the subtleties of Quintilian, the rivers of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practise hissing and panting words. What labour I spent there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I gave up, and in my eagerness to learn began again;
passages.notes: Begins mid-reference (Jerome's letter number). "meus" read as "mens" (mind); "sustinucrim" as "sustinuerim".

passages.original: Ergo cum voluntate abbatis omnia agenda sunt.] Ita ut « praeter abbatis mandatum nulla penitus vo- luntas vivat in nobis, » ut loquitur Cassianus (Lib. xii, c. 32). Haec est enim secura et unica monachis ad perfectionem tendentibus via; quam secuti sunt quotquot aliquando 66O in coenobiis enituerunt : unde etiam Regula S. Posthumio ab angelo tradita : « Si in via, inquit, calcaveris spinam, non est edu- cenda donec abbas praeceperit.
passages.english: Therefore all things are to be done with the will of the abbot.] So that "apart from the abbot's command no will at all should live in us," as Cassian says (Book 12, chapter 32). For this is the safe and only way for monks striving toward perfection, which all who have ever shone in monasteries have followed. Hence also the Rule delivered by an angel to St Posthumius: "If on the road," it says, "you tread on a thorn, it is not to be drawn out until the abbot has ordered it."
passages.notes: "66O" is a page number from the edition, omitted. St Posthumius not further identified.

passages.original: Et tamen Hildemarus hunc locum exponens, « quod dixit omnes, inquit, videtur arduum et pene difticile, eo quod multi sunt hospites qui ad monaste- rium veniunt. Sed isto modo potest intelligi : sive ideo dixit omnes hospites, quia tunc p(??)uci veniebant, sicut Cassianus dicit in collatione, et in Vita Patrum legitur, quanquam dicat S. Benedictus nanquam de- esse monasterio hospites. Potest etiam unus vel duo intelligi venisse, nam tanti tunc forte non erant sicut nunc;
passages.english: And yet Hildemar, expounding this passage, says: "His saying 'all' seems hard and almost difficult, because there are many guests who come to the monastery. But it can be understood in this way: either he said 'all guests' because few came then, as Cassian says in the Conference and as one reads in the Lives of the Fathers, although St Benedict says that guests are never lacking to a monastery. It may also be understood that one or two came, for perhaps there were not then so many as now;

passages.original: Ut ergo nuntiatus fuerit hospes, occurratur ei a priore, vel a fratribus cum omni officio charitatis.] In- cipit hic S. Benedictus hosp(??)tis suscipiendi ritum describere. Et primo quidem ante omnia vult ut ad- venienti occurratur, juxta priscorum monachorum morem, quem videre est apud Rufinum, lib. ii de Vitis Patrum, cap, 1 et 7, et insuper cap. 21, ubi de Nitriensibus; loquens, haec habet : « Huic cum appro- pinquaremus loco, ubi peregrinos fratres advenire senserunt, continuo velut examen apum, singuli qui- que ex suis cellulis proruunt, atque in obviam nobis laeto cursu et festina alacritate contendunt, portant(??)s secum quamplurimi ipsorum urceos aquae et panes, secundum quod propheta corripiens quosdam dicit, quia non existis filiis Israel in obviam cum pane et aqua.
passages.english: As soon, then, as a guest is announced, let him be met by the superior or by the brothers with every service of charity.] Here St Benedict begins to describe the rite of receiving a guest. And first, before everything, he wishes that the one arriving be met, according to the custom of the ancient monks, which may be seen in Rufinus, Lives of the Fathers book 2, chapters 1 and 7, and moreover chapter 21, where, speaking of the monks of Nitria, he says this: "As we approached this place, when they perceived that foreign brothers were arriving, at once like a swarm of bees they each rushed out of their cells and hastened to meet us with joyful running and eager speed, very many of them carrying with them jars of water and loaves, according to what the prophet says in rebuking certain people: that you did not go out to meet the children of Israel with bread and water."

passages.original: Manavit autem iste ritus ab antiquis monachis, ut docet Rufinus his verbis (Lib. iide Vitis Patr., cap. 1) : « Hic est enim mos apud Aegyptum, ut ubi adve- nerint, statim per orationem sibi invicem confoede- rentur. » Et loquens de S. Apollonio (Ibid., cap. 7) : « Ubi ingressi sumus monasterium, oratione prius, ut moris est, data, pedes nostros propriis manibus lavat. » Et de Nitriensibus : « Tunc deinde nos susce- ptos adducunt primo cum psalmis ad ecclesiam.
passages.english: This rite derived from the ancient monks, as Rufinus teaches in these words (Lives of the Fathers book 2, chapter 1): "For this is the custom in Egypt, that when [brothers] arrive, they are at once bound to one another through prayer." And speaking of St Apollonius (ibid., chapter 7): "When we entered the monastery, prayer having first been offered, as is the custom, he washed our feet with his own hands." And of the monks of Nitria: "Then, having received us, they lead us first with psalms to the church."

passages.original: Illud autem nonnisi oratione praemissa propter illusiones diabolicas exhiberi voluit; id quod ab an- tiquis item monachis didicerat, testante Rufino (Lib. iide Vitis Patr., cap. 1), quia « hic est mos apud Aegyptum, ut ubi advenerint fratres, statim per ora- tionem sibi invicem confoederentur... Propterea enim forma hujusmodi inter monachos observatur, ut si quis ad eos veniat, sive vir ille, sive mulier sit, sive senex, sive juvenis, sive ignotus, sive notus, ante omnia ut oratio fiat, ut nomen Domini invocetur, quia si fuerit aliqua transformatio daemonis, continuo oratione facta diffugiet.
passages.english: But he wished that [the kiss of peace] be offered only after prayer had been made first, because of diabolical illusions; this too he had learned from the ancient monks, as Rufinus testifies (Lives of the Fathers book 2, chapter 1), that "this is the custom in Egypt, that when brothers arrive, they are at once bound to one another through prayer... For this form is observed among the monks so that, if anyone comes to them, whether man or woman, old or young, unknown or known, before all else prayer is made and the name of the Lord is invoked, because if it is some transformation of a demon, once prayer is made it will at once flee."
passages.notes: "Illud" refers to something in the Rule not in the passage; the following context suggests the kiss (osculum).

passages.original: Primo, nomine legis divinae non solum Decalogus, aut quinque Moysis libri intelliguntur, sed utrumque Vetus et Novum Testamentum, imo « omne verbum ex lege divina sumptum quod aedificat, » inquit Bernardus Cassinensis. Quid vero absolute legendum sit, vix aliqui definiunt. Olim in Cassinensi asceterio « coram hospitibus legebantur exhortationes quaedam excer- ptae ex libris divi Gregorii papae, » ut testatur Pau- lus Augustinus a Janua. Has exhortationes sive ser- mones in Cassinensi bibliotheca vidit noster Mabillo- nius. Rodulfus abbas monasterii S. Theodorici prope Rhemos, coram Roberto Flandrensium comite, et Da- norum regina Vitam S.
passages.english: First, by the name "divine law" is understood not only the Decalogue, or the five books of Moses, but both the Old and the New Testament; indeed "every word taken from the divine law that edifies," says Bernard of Monte Cassino. But what exactly is to be read, hardly anyone defines. Formerly in the monastery of Monte Cassino "certain exhortations excerpted from the books of the holy Pope Gregory were read before guests," as Paul Augustine of Genoa testifies. These exhortations or sermons our Mabillon saw in the library of Monte Cassino. Rodulf, abbot of the monastery of St Theoderic near Reims, in the presence of Robert, count of the Flemings, and the queen of the Danes, [ordered] the Life of St
passages.notes: The sentence is completed in the following context ("Theoderici ... jussit legi"): "ordered the Life of St Theoderic to be read".

passages.original: Jejunium frangatur a priore propter hospitem.] Nam, ut dicit apud Cassianum (Collat. 21, cap. 14) abbas Theonas, « Si velit quis in fratris adventu, in quo Christum debet humanitate reficere, et gratissima susceptione complecti, austeritatem jejunii custo- dire, nonne inhumanitatis potius crimen incurrit, quam laudem aut meritum religionis acquitit? » Et abbas Moyses (Collat. 2, cap. 26) : « Satis absurdum est ut fratri, imo Christo mensam offerens, non cum eo cibum pariter sumas, et ab ejus refectione te facias alienum.
passages.english: Let the fast be broken by the prior for the sake of a guest.] For, as Abbot Theonas says in Cassian (Conference 21, ch. 14), "If someone, at the arrival of a brother, in whom he ought to refresh Christ with kindness and embrace him with a most gracious welcome, wishes to keep the strictness of his fast, does he not rather incur the charge of inhumanity than gain the praise or merit of religion?" And Abbot Moses (Conference 2, ch. 26): "It is quite absurd that, offering a table to a brother, indeed to Christ, you should not take food together with him, and should make yourself a stranger to his refreshment.
passages.notes: "acquitit" read as "acquirit".

passages.original: Primo ergo S. Pater vetat litteras absque licentia abbatis mitti aut recipi; idque ex veterum mona- chorum disciplina, quam videre est apud Cassianum lib. iv cap. 16; apud S. Basilium, hic a Smaragdo citatum; in Poenis incerti auctoris apud eumdem Ba- si ium; in Regula S. Augustini, cap. 9; S. Caesarii ad monachos, c. 15; ad virgines, c. 23, et in Reca- pitulatione, c.
passages.english: First, then, the holy Father forbids letters to be sent or received without the abbot's permission; and this from the discipline of the ancient monks, which may be seen in Cassian, book 4, ch. 16; in St Basil, cited here by Smaragdus; in the Penalties of an uncertain author found with the same Basil; in the Rule of St Augustine, ch. 9; [in] St Caesarius to monks, ch. 15; to virgins, ch. 23, and in the Recapitulation, ch.

passages.original: Tunicas ex lino gestasse testatur Cassianus; sed ex Hildemaro « tonica de lana intelligenda est esse; nam potest esse et linea tonica, el serica, sed in hoc lo(??)o videtur intelligere de lana tonicam esse debere.» Magister hebdomadariis coquinam intrantibus tunicas ex sacco, cucullas ex segestri fieri mandat in Regulae cap.
passages.english: Cassian testifies that they wore tunics of linen; but according to Hildemar "the tunic is to be understood to be of wool; for a tunic can be both linen and silk, but in this place he seems to understand that the tunic ought to be of wool." The Master orders that for the weekly servers entering the kitchen tunics be made of sackcloth and cowls of *segestre* [a coarse covering cloth], in chapter
passages.notes: "lo(??)o" read as "loco"; "el" as "et". The chapter number (81) follows in the context.

passages.original: Femoralia quoque Mo- lismensibus abstulit S. Robertus, ut scribit Orderi- cus Vitalis Hist. eccles. lib. viii. Idem de Cistercien- sibus et Cassinensibus sui temporis docet Bernardus Cassinensis. Imo de Cassinensibus nostra aetate ita scribit Paulus Augustinus a Janua : « In congrega- tione nostra Cassinensi usque ad nostram aetatem vidimus senes non utentes femoralibus intra mona- sterium, sed interiorem vestem ultra genua defluen- tem ipsis genibus alligabant.
passages.english: St Robert also took away drawers from the monks of Molesme, as Orderic Vitalis writes in the Ecclesiastical History, book 8. Bernard of Monte Cassino reports the same of the Cistercians and the Cassinese of his time. Indeed, of the Cassinese in our own age Paul Augustine of Genoa writes thus: "In our Cassinese congregation, up to our own time, we have seen old men not using drawers within the monastery, but they tied the inner garment, which hung down below the knees, to the knees themselves.

passages.original: Vensa abbatis cum hospitibus et peregrinis sit semper, etc.] Inter bospites et peregrinos hic distinguunt com- mentatores. Hildemarus : « Hospites, inquit, sunt qui de eadem regione sunt de prope. Peregrini sunt qui de alia regione; peregrinus enim dicitur, sicut dicit Cassiodorus, quasi pergens longius. » Idem habet Bernardus Cassinensis, cujus verba cum retu- lisset in primo commentario Boherius, addit : « Vel dicuntur peregrini qui ad monasterium aut locum aliquem devotionis causa declinant;
passages.english: Let the abbot's table always be with the guests and pilgrims, etc.] Here the commentators distinguish between guests and pilgrims. Hildemar: "Guests," he says, "are those who are from the same region, from nearby. Pilgrims are those who are from another region; for *peregrinus* is so called, as Cassiodorus says, as if 'going further' (*pergens longius*)." Bernard of Monte Cassino has the same, and Boherius, having quoted his words in his first commentary, adds: "Or those are called pilgrims who turn aside to a monastery or some place for the sake of devotion;
passages.notes: "Vensa" read as "Mensa"; "bospites" as "hospites".

passages.original: Aliis vero placuit decem probationis constituere dies, de quibus Cassianus : « Ambiens quis intra coe- nobii recipi disciplinam, non ante prorsus admitti- tur, quam diebus decem, vel eo amplius pro foribus excubans, judicium perseverantiae ac desiderii sui, pariterque humilitatis ac patientia* demonstraverit. » Atque ita in Regula vivendi monachis a S. Davide praecripta (In ejus Vita, apud boll., 1 Martii), « qui sancto proposito a mundo se convertens fratrum inire consortium affectabat, prius decem diebus prae foribus monasterii, quasi reprobatus et verborum opprobriis conviciatus, remanebat.
passages.english: Others, however, chose to set ten days of probation, about which Cassian [says]: "Someone seeking to be received into the discipline of the monastery is not admitted at all until, keeping watch before the doors for ten days or more, he has shown proof of his perseverance and desire, and likewise of his humility and patience." And so in the Rule of life prescribed for monks by St David (in his Life, in the Bollandists, 1 March): "Whoever, turning from the world with holy purpose, sought to enter the fellowship of the brothers, first remained ten days before the doors of the monastery, as if rejected and assailed with reproachful words.

passages.original: 1) : « Si aliquam in cellulam vo- luerit inferre substantiam, in mensa ponatur coram omnibus fratribus, velut Regula continet. Quod si susceptus fuerit, non solum de substantia quam in- tulit, sed nec de seipso ab illa judicabit hora. » Quae totidem verbis continentur in Regula sancti Macarii (Cap. 4). Idem docet sanctus Basilius in Regula a Rufino translata exemplo Jacobi et Joannis, qui patrem suum et navem in qua erant reliquerunt; et sancti Matthaei, qui vectigal ut sequeretur Christum abjecit; id quod fuse prosequitur in Regulis fus. cap.
passages.english: 1): "If he wishes to bring any property into the cell, let it be placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule contains. But if he has been received, from that hour he will have no say, not only over the property he brought, but not even over himself." These things are contained in just as many words in the Rule of St Macarius (ch. 4). St Basil teaches the same in the Rule translated by Rufinus, by the example of James and John, who left their father and the boat in which they were; and of St Matthew, who cast aside the customs-post to follow Christ; which he pursues at length in the Longer Rules, ch.
passages.notes: The opening "1)" completes a chapter reference begun in the preceding context (Third Rule of the Holy Fathers, ch. 1). "judicabit" taken as "will have judgement/authority".

passages.original: Benedictus autem aut pauperibus erogari, aut facta solemniter donatione, monasterio conferri hona novitiorum constituit : sed postremum istud summa districtione cavebant Tabennenses Aegyptii- que monachi, qui, ut scribit Cassianus (Lib.iv, c. 4), « idcirco ne usibus quidem coenobii profuturas susci- pere ab co (novitio) pecunias acquiescunt. Primum ne confidentia hujus oblationis inflatus nequaquam se pauperioribus fratribus coaequare dignetur. Tum ne per hanc oblationem nullatenus ad humilitatem Christi descendens, cum sub disciplina coenobii non potuerit perdurare, egressus exinde, ea quae in prin- cipio renuntiationis suae spirituali fervore succensus intulerat, tepefactus postea, non sine injuria mona- sterii, sacrilego spiritu recipere atque exigere molia- tur;
passages.english: Benedict, however, laid down that the goods of novices should either be distributed to the poor or, after a solemn donation has been made, be conferred on the monastery; but this last the Tabennesiots and the Egyptian monks guarded against with the utmost strictness, who, as Cassian writes (book 4, ch. 4), "for this reason do not consent to accept money from him (the novice) even if it would serve the uses of the monastery. First, lest, puffed up by confidence in this offering, he should not deign to make himself equal to the poorer brothers. Then, lest, not descending through this offering to the humility of Christ, when he cannot endure under the discipline of the monastery and leaves it, he should afterwards, grown lukewarm, try with a sacrilegious spirit, not without injury to the monastery, to recover and demand back what he had brought in at the beginning of his renunciation, kindled with spiritual fervour;
passages.notes: "hona" read as "bona"; "co" as "eo".

passages.original: Contra autem hoc est et periculosum monachis, et quod eos potest reddere imbecilles, et virtutum carentes fructibus; naro nec planta quidem potest ferre fructus quae as- sidue transplantatur. » Ita apud Cassianum abbas Ne- steros (Collat. 14, cap. 5) : « Unicuique utile atque con- veniens est, ut secundum propositum quod elegit, sive gratiam quam accepit, summo studio ac diligen- tia ad operis arrepti perfectionem pervenire festinet, et aliorum quidem laudans, admiransque virtutes, ne- quaquam a sua, quam elegit, professione discedat. » Ita S. Anselmus ad La(??)zonem monachum, qui talia forte meditabatur, scribens, fuse et eleganter hoc pro- sequitur argumentum, respondetque omnibus quae adversus hanc sententiam proferri possent.
passages.english: But this, on the contrary, is both dangerous for monks and something that can make them weak and lacking the fruits of virtues; for not even a plant that is constantly transplanted can bear fruit." So in Cassian Abbot Nesteros (Conference 14, ch. 5): "It is useful and fitting for each one that, according to the purpose he has chosen or the grace he has received, he should hasten with the greatest zeal and diligence to reach the perfection of the work he has taken up, and, while praising and admiring the virtues of others, should by no means depart from his own profession which he has chosen." So St Anselm, writing to the monk La[n]zo, who was perhaps contemplating such things, pursues this argument at length and elegantly, and answers everything that could be brought forward against this view.
passages.notes: "naro" read as "nam". The monk's name is partly illegible ("La(??)zonem"); probably Lanzo.

passages.original: Tandem Petrus abbas Cel- lensis variis comparationibus idem demonstrat (Lib.ix, epist. 12) : « Ranas et muscas inquietantes pene- tralia cordis vestri utinam vos abjicere vel potius exterminare brevi admonitione possem! Non ignoro apud Aristotelem dubitare de singulis non esse inu- tile. Teneo autem apud Hippocratem quod mu atio- nes maximae generant morbos. Dicit Gregorius quod plantae quae saepe transponuntur radices non mit- tunt..... In parabola 811 quoque Evangelii dum fatuae virgines irent emere oleum, clausa est janua.
passages.english: Finally Peter, abbot of Celle, demonstrates the same thing by various comparisons (Book 9, letter 12): "If only I could, by a brief admonition, cast out, or rather exterminate, the frogs and flies that disturb the inner chambers of your heart! I am not unaware that according to Aristotle it is not useless to raise doubts about particular things. But I hold with Hippocrates that the greatest changes produce diseases. Gregory says that plants which are often transplanted do not put down roots..... In the parable of the Gospel too, while the foolish virgins were going to buy oil, the door was shut."
passages.notes: "mu atio- nes" read as mutationes. "811" is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: Porro non solum monachis, sed i(??)sis etiam ethni- cis sacratus fuit senio i(??)a surgendi usus : « Omni seniori, inquit Aristoteles (Lib.ixEthic., cap. 2), honor pro aetate reddendus est assurgendo, et ses- sione cedendo, atque hujusmodi caeteris. » Et Cicero (De Senectute) : « Lacedaemonii venientibus senibus omnes in theatro assurgere solebant, et eos sessum recipere.
passages.english: Moreover, the custom of rising for the old was held sacred not only by monks but even by the pagans themselves: "To every elder," says Aristotle (Ethics, Book 9, chapter 2), "honour must be paid according to his age, by rising, by giving up one's seat, and by other things of this kind." And Cicero (On Old Age): "The Spartans, when old men came in, all used to rise in the theatre and receive them into a seat."
passages.notes: Scanning damage: "i(??)sis" read as ipsis, "senio i(??)a" as seniori (or senioribus) assurgendi.

passages.original: Non comparat divus Pater partem minorem majori, sed partem toti : dicit illum essa declarandum abbatem quem vel tota communitas elegerit, vel saltem pars sanioris consilii, licet parva, hoc est pars cui plures subscripserunt, licet pauci. Exemplo res clarior evadet : Dantur viginti activae voces; si omnes Petro faveant, nulli est quaestioni locus. Si ipsi faveant quatuor, Joanni septem, Paul(??) sex, et Ambrosio reliquae : vult institutor sanctissimus praeponi Joannem : quamvis enim sit parva congre- gationis pars quae illum elegit, numerosior tamen est aliis, et propterea sanior praesumitur. » Econtra Pau- lus Augustinus a Janua monachus Cassinas, quam Caramuel fere omnium esse dicit interpretationem, et tamen reprobat, propius ad S.
passages.english: The holy Father does not compare a smaller part with a larger, but a part with the whole: he says that the one is to be declared abbot whom either the whole community has elected, or at least the part of sounder counsel, though small, that is, the part to which more have subscribed, though they are few. The matter will become clearer by an example. Suppose there are twenty active votes. If all favour Peter, there is no room for question. If four favour him, seven John, six Paul, and the rest Ambrose, the most holy founder wishes John to be set over [them]; for although the part of the community that elected him is small, it is nevertheless more numerous than the others, and is therefore presumed sounder." On the other hand Paulus Augustinus of Genoa, a monk of Monte Cassino, [rejects] this interpretation, which Caramuel says is that of almost everyone and yet rejects, [and] closer to St.
passages.notes: "essa" read as esse. The final sentence is incomplete and continues beyond the passage; its syntax is awkward, possibly garbled in transmission.

passages.original: Pater qualem velit in abbatem eligi, nimirum aliquem vitae merito et sapientiae doctrina inclytum; nam, etsi « coenobitae sufficiat vitae meritum, ut loquitur Boherius, sapien- tiae tamen habere doctrinam convenit abbatem. » Hic enim locum habere potest illud S. Hieronymi : « San- cta rusticitas quantum ex vitae merito aedificat Ec- clesiam Christi, tantum nocet, si destruentibus non resistat. » Resistere autem non potest, nisi fuerit sapientiae doctrina instructus.
passages.english: [Here St. Benedict, the] Father, declares what sort of person he wishes to be elected abbot: namely someone distinguished by merit of life and learning in wisdom; for although "merit of life suffices for a cenobite," as Boherius puts it, "it is fitting that the abbot should have learning in wisdom." For here that saying of St. Jerome can apply: "Holy rusticity, as much as it builds up the Church of Christ by the merit of its life, does that much harm if it does not resist those who destroy [it]." But he cannot resist unless he is instructed in learning of wisdom.

passages.original: Oporet ergo eum esse doctum lege divina.] Etsi « constet neminem prorsus ob imperitiam litterarum a perfectione cordis excludi, nec rusticitatem obesse ad capessendam cordis atque animae puritatem, » ut loquitur Cassianus (Collat. 10, cap. 14); imo cum saepe « scientia saecularis, teste S. Bernardo (Serm. 9, in Cant.), inebriet curiositate, non charitate, im- pleas, non nutriens, inf(??)ans, non aedificans, ingurgi- tans, non confortans;
passages.english: Therefore he must be learned in the divine law.] Although "it is established that no one at all is excluded from perfection of heart through ignorance of letters, and that rusticity is no obstacle to attaining purity of heart and soul," as Cassian says (Conference 10, chapter 14); indeed, although "secular knowledge," as St. Bernard testifies (Sermon 9 on the Song of Songs), often "intoxicates with curiosity, not with charity, filling but not nourishing, puffing up but not building up, gorging but not strengthening;
passages.notes: "inf(??)ans" read as inflans. Sentence continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: Memineritque calamum quassatum non conterendum.] 844 « Id est monachum, inquit Smaragdus, macu- lis peccatorum confectum, variisque vitiis conqu(??)s- satum, ad desperationis foveam, vel fugae lapsum non impellendum. Calamum enim quassatum sine dubio conterit, qui peccatori non salutis, sed perdi- tionis praebet occasionem. Hanc B. Hieronymus ait (In Matth.xii) : Qui peccatori non porrigit, nec por- tat οnu(??) fratris sui, iste quassatum c(??)damum confrin- g(??)t. » Id quod duobus fic(??)i docet Richardus de S. Angelo : « 1° Si per superfluam remissionem seu immoderatam dimittitur peccatum, et sic incurrit laqueum perpetuae mortis;
passages.english: And let him remember that the bruised reed is not to be broken.] "That is," says Smaragdus, "a monk worn down by the stains of sins and bruised by various vices is not to be driven into the pit of despair or into the fall of flight. For he without doubt breaks the bruised reed who offers a sinner an occasion not of salvation but of perdition. This is what blessed Jerome says (On Matthew 12): He who does not stretch out [his hand] to a sinner, nor carry his brother's burden, breaks the bruised reed." Richard of Sant'Angelo teaches that this happens in two ways: "1st, if the sin is forgiven by excessive or immoderate remission, and so he falls into the snare of everlasting death;
passages.notes: "844" is a page number, omitted. Scanning damage read as conquassatum, onus, calamum, confringit, fieri.

passages.original: Pistrinum.] De quo Hildemarus : « Pistrinum quasi pilitrinum, qui » pilo antea tundebant granum : unde et apud veteres non molitores, sed pistores dicti, quasi pinsores, a pinsandis granis frumenti; molae enim usus nondum erat, sed granum pilo findebant : unde et Virgilius :
passages.english: Bakehouse.] On which Hildemar [says]: "Pistrinum [bakehouse], as if pilitrinum, [from those] who formerly pounded grain with a pestle; hence among the ancients they were called not millers but pistores, as if pinsores, from pounding the grains of wheat; for the use of the mill did not yet exist, but they split the grain with a pestle. Hence also Virgil:
passages.notes: The etymologies play on Latin words (pilum, pestle; pinsere, to pound). The Virgil quotation is not included in the passage.

passages.original: 95) : « Omnia necessaria intus intra regias esse oportet, id est, furnum, macinae, refrigerium, hortus, et omnia necessaria, ut non sit frequens occasio, propter quam fratres multoties foras egressi, saecu- laribus mixti, forte a religiosorum oculis visi, ad damnationem potius nostram ab eis pro angelis adoremur, et benedicite nobis non mentis indigna dicatur. » Atque haec erat veterum monachorum praxis, quam videre est apud Rufinum, de monaste- rio Isidori abbatis sic loquentem (Lib.iide Vitis Patr. cap. 17) : « Vidimus et apud Thebaidam etiam Isi- dori nominatissimum monasterium, amplissimis spa- tiis circumseptum, muroque circumdatum, in quo habitantibus viris larga praebebantur habitacula. Intrinsecus putei plures, horti irrigui, omnium quo- que pomorum arborumque paradisi, 866 quaecun- que necessaria usibus erant, sufficienter, imo et abundanter provisa;
passages.english: 95): "All necessary things ought to be inside, within the gates, that is, oven, mills, cooling-place, garden, and all necessities, so that there may not be frequent occasion for the brothers to go out many times, mingle with seculars, and perhaps, seen by the eyes of the religious [i.e. by lay people], be revered by them as angels to our damnation, and an unworthy 'bless us' be said to us." And this was the practice of the ancient monks, as can be seen in Rufinus, speaking thus of the monastery of Abbot Isidore (Lives of the Fathers, Book 2, chapter 17): "We saw also in the Thebaid the very famous monastery of Isidore, enclosed in very ample grounds and surrounded by a wall, in which spacious dwellings were provided for the men living there. Inside were several wells, irrigated gardens, [and] a paradise of all fruits and trees; whatever was necessary for use was provided sufficiently, indeed abundantly;
passages.notes: "regias" probably for januas or similar (gates); "macinae" taken as mills. The clause "a religiosorum oculis visi" is obscure, perhaps corrupt. "866" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: 109, quod piscibus aqua, hoc monachis claustrum : quemadmodum ergo piscis extra aquam cito exstin- guitur, sic monachos extra monasterium facillime perit : adeo ut non mirum sit quosdam Patres etiam consolandorum parentum causa egressum e claustro suis denegasse. Praeclarum habemus ea de re Petri Blesensis in praefata epistola testimonium : « Juxta doctrinam Hieronymi : Sis honestus in domo, sis rarus in publico, si aegrotaverit aut obierit aliquis de tuis parentibus, non sit tibi eorum aegritudo, vel mors egressionis occasio; sine mortuos sepelire mortuos suos. Fallax et proditoria est affectio parentelae. Carnalis amor extra Dei amorem cito te capiet, et affectio mundi, quae jam in te aruerat, in pernicem animi revirescet. » Multa jam ea de re diximus ad cap.
passages.english: 109: what water is to fish, the cloister is to monks: just as a fish quickly dies out of water, so a monk very easily perishes outside the monastery; so that it is no wonder that some Fathers refused their monks leave to go out of the cloister even for the sake of consoling their parents. We have a splendid testimony on this matter from Peter of Blois in the aforesaid letter: "According to the teaching of Jerome: be honourable at home, be rare in public; if any of your relatives falls ill or dies, let their illness or death not be an occasion for you to go out; let the dead bury their dead. Affection for kin is deceitful and treacherous. Carnal love apart from the love of God will quickly seize you, and the affection for the world, which had already withered in you, will grow green again to the ruin of your soul." We have already said much on this matter at chapter
passages.notes: "monachos" read as monachus; "pernicem" as perniciem.

passages.original: Infirmitates suas sive corporum, sive morum, patien- tissime tolerent.] En secundum boni zeli exercitium, quod commendat apud Cassianum abbas Joannes his verbis (Collat. 19, c. 9) : « Is vere et non ex parte perfectus est, qui et in eremo squalorem soli- tudinis et in coenobio infirmitates aequali magnani- mitate sustentat. » Et S. Bernardus (Serm. 12 in Cant.) : « Omnis in vohis, qui fraternas infirmi- tates tam corporum quam animorum non solum patienter supportat, sed insuper, si licet, et si valet, juvat obsequiis, confortat alloquiis, consiliis infor- mat;
passages.english: Let them bear most patiently one another's infirmities, whether of body or of character.] Here is the second exercise of good zeal, which Abbot John commends in Cassian in these words (Conference 19, chapter 9): "He is truly, and not partly, perfect who bears with equal magnanimity both the squalor of solitude in the desert and infirmities in the monastery." And St. Bernard (Sermon 12 on the Song of Songs): "Everyone among you who not only patiently supports the infirmities of the brothers, both of body and of soul, but moreover, if it is allowed and if he is able, helps by services, strengthens by words, instructs by counsels;
passages.notes: "vohis" read as vobis. Sentence continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: » 2° In timore, amore, cultuque Creatoris, juxta illud ejus- dem Ambrosii (Ibid., c. 45) : « Honestum est, Do- mine, ut te timeamus, te diligamus, te deprecemur et honoremus : te enim decet hymnus in Sion. » 3° In disciplinata conversatione exteriori, secundum illud Regulae S. Augustini : « In incessu, statu, habitu vestro, et in omnibus motibus vestris, nihil fiat quod cujusquam offendat aspectum, sed quod vestram decet sanctitatem. »
passages.english: 2nd, in the fear, love and worship of the Creator, according to that saying of the same Ambrose (ibid., ch. 45): "It is honourable, Lord, that we should fear you, love you, entreat and honour you: for a hymn befits you in Zion." 3rd, in a disciplined outward conduct, according to that saying of the Rule of St Augustine: "In your gait, your bearing, your dress, and in all your movements, let nothing be done that might offend anyone's sight, but [only] what befits your holiness."
passages.notes: The opening » closes a quotation begun in the preceding context (Ambrosian citation on the flight from vices).

passages.original: Quae enim pagina, aut quis sermo divinae auctoritatis Veteris ac Novi Testamenti, etc... hoc non resonat, ut recto cursu perveniamus ad Creatorem nostrum?] Istud praeclare resonabat apud Cassianum abbas Pynufius, cum compendiosam ad perfectionem viam demon- strans, et ascendentes ad ipsam charitatem, quae Deus est, gradus componens diceret (Lib.iv, c. 43) : « Audi paucis ordinem per quem ascendere ad perfectionem summam sine ullo labore ac difficultate valeas.
passages.english: For what page, or what utterance of divine authority in the Old and New Testament, etc., does not echo this, that we should arrive by a straight course at our Creator?] This was splendidly echoed in Cassian by Abbot Pinufius, when, showing a short road to perfection and setting out the steps that ascend to charity itself, which is God, he said (Book IV, ch. 43): "Hear in a few words the order by which you may be able to ascend to the highest perfection without any toil or difficulty.
passages.notes: The first sentence, ending in ], is the quoted lemma from the Rule of St Benedict (ch. 73) on which the commentary comments. Pynufius = Pinufius, abbot in Cassian's Institutes.

passages.original: Quod vero S. Benedictus eum vocat Patrem et suum, non inde sequitur eum militasse sub S. Basilii institutis; sed eum Patrem appellat, vel honoris gra- tia tanquam antiquiorem, juxta illud S. Augustini : « Honorificentiae causa Patres appellamus eos qui nos vel tempore vel meritis praecesserunt; nam illud honoris est, quod quotidie senibus dicamus Pater. » Vel quia, ut ait S. Hieronymus : « Vulgato sermone maxime in Palaestina et Aegypti monasteriis se invi- cem Patres vocant. » Unde Cyrillus episcopus Alex- andrinus epistolam ad presbyteros et diaconos missam, quae habetur in actis concilii Ephesini, in- scripsit Patribus monachis. Vel denique quia nomen Patris praestantissimis Ecclesiae scriptoribus, inter quos haud erat inferior S.
passages.english: But the fact that St Benedict calls him 'Father' and 'our' does not imply that he served under the institutes of St Basil; rather he calls him Father either out of honour, as one more ancient, according to that saying of St Augustine: "For the sake of respect we call 'Fathers' those who have preceded us either in time or in merits; for it is a matter of honour that we daily say 'Father' to old men." Or because, as St Jerome says: "In common speech, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, they call one another Fathers." Hence Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, addressed a letter sent to the priests and deacons, which is found in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, 'to the Fathers, the monks'. Or finally because the name of Father was customarily given to the most eminent writers of the Church, among whom St
passages.notes: Latin 'Patrem et suum' likely reflects the Rule's phrase 'Regula sancti Patris nostri Basilii' (ch. 73). The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the next context reads 'Basil was not the least', citing Haeftenus.
